speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I think a word should be
said to the effect that this resolution and the bill based upon it are indeed welcome. As a matter of fact those interested in the welfare of our blind persons have for a considerable time been requesting that the legislation respecting the blind be put in a statute separate from the legislation respecting our elder citizens. I take it the reason for that request is the force of circumstances.
Indeed, now that the old age pension plan is being put on a different basis it becomes necessary that our legislation respecting blind allowances be taken out of the existing legislation and put in a statute by itself. That, I take it, is also made necessary by reason of the fact that the resolution we passed a few moments ago specifies that the federal government shall pay 50 per cent of the pension paid to those from 65 to 69. Obviously in respect of blind persons it would be unfair to the provinces to put that division into effect. Rather it is only fair to the provinces that the present relationship

of a payment of 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the provinces should be continued.
I take it however that although this bill will meet the requests of those interested in blind persons, so far as it goes, in that it separates their legislation from old age pension legislation, there is nothing in the bill to be based on the resolution which makes any change in substance so far as allowances for blind persons are concerned. Could the minister say whether that is so? So far as matters of substance are concerned, will the bill simply carry forward what is now in our legislation respecting the blind?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Could the minister answer my question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I wished to make sure no one else wished to speak. If no one else is speaking I will say briefly this, that my hon. friend has welcomed with pleasure, as I am sure the country will generally, this measure separating assistance given to blind persons from assistance given to the aged. This is in keeping with the request made to me by the various organizations representing the blind over the period of the last few years.
Unlike the bill based on the resolution we have just passed, the contribution of the federal government in this instance is not, despite the higher commitments involved in the total program, being reduced. It continues at 75 per cent.
I am not so sure after listening to my hon. friend this morning whether he and I will agree as to what changes of substance mean. But certainly as I understand the word he will find that the bill when presented does have very important modifications that are changes of substance and that will improve the situation so far as blind persons are concerned.
In any event my hon. friend will realize that, as in the other instance, the extent to which we have taken action in the bill is largely dependent upon the agreement we were able to obtain with the provinces whose financial responsibility in these matters varies in accordance with the terms, particularly, of the permissible income section.

In connection with the permissible income section I suggest there are one or two changes which should be made, and which I would ask the minister to consider. I refer to blind farmers. As the minister and other hon. members know, there is no set income formula on the farm. In one year there may be a profit while in the next year there may be a loss. If a farmer has a profit in one year his pension is cut, whereas

in the next year he may have a loss and there is no increase in the pension.
Blind farmers have suggested to me that I bring to the attention of the minister the necessity for the levelling off of incomes for pension purposes, as it is done for income tax purposes. This seems to be a reasonable request. People who are farming, and who have all their senses, are having a bad enough time; but for blind farmers it is worse.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure there is nothing controversial in the bill, and I am sure hon. members will be in complete agreement that anything suggested for the benefit of these unfortunate people who happen to be blind should be done. I do not think there is anything to be said at the present time, or that anything need be said until we have the bill before us. I cannot see any reason for further debate, because I believe we are all in complete agreement.
How many blind persons, from the age of 21, on, will come under this measure?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
We estimate there are about
18,000	blind persons in the country and, roughly, 11,000 between the ages of 21 and 69.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF MEMBERS-POWER TO CONSTRUCT RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
Is the Prime Minister going to make a statement at this point?
Federal District Commission Act

subtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER OF MEMBERS-POWER TO CONSTRUCT RAILWAYS, ETC.
speechtext:
I had not intended making any statement as the resolution is quite selfexplanatory. There are three points dealt with in the resolution. First, it is intended to increase the members of the commission by one. By the 1946 amendment it was provided that there would be a member on the commission representing each of the provinces, and the number provided for was nine. It is felt that Newfoundland now being one of the provinces should also have a representative on the commission. The first purpose of the bill to be founded on this resolution is to make provision for the appointment of a member to represent the province of Newfoundland.
The second purpose is to take advantage of the fact that we are amending the act to provide for something which has heretofore been provided for by a dollar item in the estimates. In the 1950 estimates and again in the estimates for this year a dollar item was provided to authorize the federal district commission to carry on that part of the recommendations of the joint committee that had to do with providing facilities to improve the railway situation in Ottawa and ultimately to do away with the trackage that leads into the Union station in the heart of the city. It being necessary to amend the act it was felt that it would be more proper to have this in the act itself rather than to rely from year to year upon the dollar item in the estimates.
The third has to do with Gatineau park. Gatineau park is planned to include an area something over 70,000 acres, and some
30,000	acres or more have already been acquired in rural municipalities. The assessment and taxes on these lands would have amounted to something less than $5,000 distributed among a few rural municipalities While that amount is not large it is felt that there was some hardship on those municipalities to decrease their tax revenue from the land to be included in the national park out of which they do not derive any special benefit at the present time. The bill to be founded on the resolution will empower the federal district commission to make grants to these local municipalities not exceeding what the taxes would have been before the lands were taken over to form part of the park.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall deal first with the remarks of the leader of the opposition. I think both he and I read the same newspaper. I was a bit concerned the other day, as possibly he was, when I read that article saying that so long as Mr. Bronson was chairman of the commission there would be no cause for anxiety as to the extent to which the powers of the federal district commission might be exercised, but that it might be that under the legislation to be proposed they were going to have power to enter into businesses that might go beyond what was really required for their purposes. I immediately got out the bill to see whether there was anything to justify apprehension of that kind and I found that there was not. This is strictly related to the implementation of the recommendations of the joint committee with respect to the changing of the railway location.
Since I have mentioned his name I should like to take this opportunity to express on behalf of the government, and I think on behalf of all members of the house, very sincere appreciation of the great devotion which Mr. Bronson has brought over the years to the implementation of the recommendations of the joint committee of the two houses of parliament. I do concur with the writer of an article which I saw in a newspaper the other day, no matter how extensive the powers may be, as long as they are being exercised under the control of Mr. Bronson no one will have any occasion for anxiety. In addition, however, I think that the terms of the statute are such that there is not apt to be any conflict with any municipal authorities. Frequently there are discussions with the municipal authorities, and it took some time to reach an agreement upon the contribution that the city of Ottawa would make to the bridge now being constructed over the railway yards in the heart of the 

city. But that has been settled by an agreement which I think is working out very satisfactorily both for the federal district commission and for the civic authorities.
I think it would be proper for me to say at this time that the federal district commission has had the fullest possible co-operation from the municipal authorities of the city of Ottawa and from the municipal authorities of the other municipalities having territory within the federal district. It is for the purpose of maintaining these good relations that the commission feels that it should make grants to those rural municipalities, with respect to the large areas that are being taken over for the Gatineau park that would be such as not to occasion them, at least until such time as the park is completed and in operation and they derive some benefits therefrom, any loss in their municipal taxation.
I think all who are interested in the development of the capital owe a debt to the chairman and members of the federal district commission for the manner in which they have succeeded in enlisting the good will and in conserving good relations not only with the municipal authorities but also with the people of the districts where the work is being carried on. I think it is a very happy example of the kind of co-operation that can be brought about between different levels of government, and I should like to include in my tribute an expression of gratitude for the co-operation that has been obtained from the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec. I think that at every level there has been the most satisfactory degree of co-operation and helpfulness to each other that could be desired in carrying out that kind of a plan. It seems to me that it is being felt by them as it has been felt in every quarter of this house that what is being done here is something of national scope that will be a source of satisfaction and pride for every Canadian citizen.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, every year on
these estimates I have usually made an appeal for a national health plan for Canada. In fact I have made this appeal year after year on behalf of this party. At times I have thought that these continuous appeals would become tiresome to members of the house, but I came into the house in 1945 with the idea in mind that I would try to do something for the people of this country by attempting to add my voice to those who felt that a national health plan for Canada was a necessity. Year after year since that time, and two or three times a year, on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party I have spoken on the necessity of a health plan for Canada, a plan that would bring treatment to every person in Canada no matter in what district he or she resides. But I was amazed last night to read in the evening press the remarks made by one of the cabinet ministers in the Waterloo by-election campaign. I am perfectly aware that in general elections or in by-elections parties debate certain
Supply-Health and Welfare things to their own advantage, but in this case when it comes to a matter of the policy of a party that is an entirely different thing. I admit we have all made statements for our parties and that we have argued in election campaigns, but this thing seems to be something entirely different in that it affects the policy of this party. Before entering into any discussion, however, I intend to again clarify the position of this party as far as national health insurance is concerned. I intend to quote from an article which appeared in the Toronto Telegram of June 20. The Telegram was absolutely fair at that time; the Liberal meetings were covered by one correspondent, the account of the C.C.F. meetings was written by another, and the Conservative meetings were covered by still another. I was amazed to read what the minister of immigration had said at a meeting in New Hamburg. The first matter he dealt with was export markets, and that was perfectly normal. But I am going to read some of this report dealing with the second matter he referred to, and some of it is in quotation marks:
He assured his farmer audience that the government is soon to propose a national health scheme-[DOT] as promised earlier-and he added that he expected the Progressive Conservatives would "oppose it at first, then try to take credit for it after."

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Lanark has the floor.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am going to quote from a
speech I made in this house on June 30, 1948, when the matter of national health grants was being brought into the picture. Hon. members will remember that national health grants were announced by the Prime Minister in May, 1948, but we did not get around to discussing them until the last day of that session, which was June 30. At that time I said:
In May the Prime Minister announced increased grants for national health. We welcomed the introduction of a plan that would help out national

Supply-Health and Welfare health. The Progressive Conservative party, realizing this need, has long urged a broader program for national health and for increased grants. During the time I have been a member of this house we have repeatedly drawn the attention of the members of the house to the urgent necessity of action to overcome the deficiencies in our national health services. No later than March of this year I spoke on this matter in the house; I stated that the time had come to enunciate and put into effect a national health program for Canada. I further stated that the objective plan of this party was one which would bring health services to every Canadian citizen regardless of race, economic status or geographical position.
Then I went on to deal with the matter of the health grants:
A year ago I drew the attention of the house to the necessity of a national stocktaking with regard to health. There is nothing new in the program that has been introduced. We welcome it and we welcome the increased grants. I believe that every member of this house, regardless of his political affiliation, approves any measure which will cut down mortality rates and relieve human suffering. Consideration of national health measures and anything that will better the condition of the people in regard to national health should be far above any political considerations.
I simply want to put on record that through the years, and certainly since 1945 when I came into this house, this party has advocated a national health program for Canada. I personally have advocated it at every opportunity. So in regard to this statement I thought our position should be made clear as far as national health is concerned. Sometimes these matters do become open to debate, and sometimes government members or even opposition members make certain statements for the sake of their party. In connection with national health grants and grants to hospitals I remember a speech made on the budget last spring by the hon. member for Mount Royal, a gentleman for whom I have the highest regard but who, I am quite sure, misunderstood the situation. At page 2328 of Hansard for April 24 of this year the hon. member said:
Another important medium of communication is the field of public relations. Are we doing a job in this field? No one will accuse the Department of National Health and Welfare of hiding its light under a bushel nor should they do so because their work is both instructional and educational. But how many persons realize that in the last two years, through the initiative of the department, the federal government has been responsible for the construction of 27,000 new hospital beds, many of them in my own constituency, in a total of 40,000? I doubt if the people of this country realize the revolution which has been brought about, nationally speaking, in national health and public welfare owing to the initiative and research policies of the department.
I am sure the minister himself would refute that statement in what was otherwise a really good speech. I feel sure the hon. member for Mount Royal misunderstood the whole situation when he suggested that this

department was responsible for providing
27,000	hospital beds. I have mentioned this matter on other occasions. In my own province of Ontario grants are given for the construction of hospital beds, and the grants given by this department do not begin to cover the cost of constructing hospitals. I remember that in a speech some time ago on the estimates of this department I pointed out that in this province the average cost of a hospital bed, over and above any grants that might be made, was something like $7,500. That is in addition to the amount given by the federal government and, in our case, the provincial government. I am familiar with what is happening in one town in my own constituency, where they are working on the idea of building a hospital. This town has a population of 5,000; they are very anxious for a hospital, but the question of financing has made it very difficult. In order to keep this matter clear, while we certainly approve of the grants given under the health plan, at the present time it is difficult for municipalities to obtain the money necessary to build a hospital. It is a difficult job to raise the thousands of dollars required, because hospital construction is very expensive.
I was rather pleased yesterday to read of some of the research being carried on at the present time. This was brought out at a meeting of the Canadian Medical Association in Montreal. It may be of interest to hon. members to learn that 2,000 doctors at a convention in Montreal were able to witness by television operations performed in various hospitals, some of them a mile or more away. Apparently the television camera was placed above the operating table, and thus they were able to get a view that would be open only to a doctor assisting at the operation. This, of course, has nothing to do with the Department of National Health and Welfare or the consideration of these grants, but it does show what progress is being made and indicates that some of the things being discovered now will mean a great deal to the medical profession in future and, by means of further education, will be of assistance to those who may be suffering.
There are some needs in this country that should be fully discussed. I have mentioned one, the need for hospital beds and the difficulties municipalities find in providing them. If we are to carry on a program of making treatment available to everyone, "then it will be necessary to have a further program in connection with hospital accommodation. It is necessary that we should make treatment available to every person. Conditions in the medical profession and in hospitals are rapidly changing. New discoveries have produced new methods of treatment. Some of

the diseases which used to cause concern to medical men have now been defeated by research and the advent of new forms of drugs. But this is going to bring about an entirely different situation, and we are rapidly coming to it.
The life span of people in this country is becoming longer, owing to these discoveries. We are now able to cope with diseases which we formerly could not do anything with in the matter of treatment. People are therefore going to live longer. We are going to have a class of older citizens. If we have this class of older citizens it is obvious that, when their life span runs out, they will die of some disease; and it will probably be some disease in connection with old age, probably disease of the cardiovascular system. You are going to have more people who die of strokes, heart disease and possibly cancer.
In considering the question of hospital accommodation for the future, we should consider this matter, because it is difficult to obtain accommodation for completely disabled aged persons owing to the fact that they usually suffer a long, lingering breakdown of health. That situation exists in all of the hospitals in the country and in the wards of the hospitals across the country. In every men's ward and in every women's ward there are some of these older people for whom there is no other place. If it is possible to get them into a rest home, that can be done. But few of these municipalities have rest homes for these elderly people. In the future we must therefore look forward to an entirely different class of disease existing among old people. Not only that, but we must make some arrangement to provide accommodation for them.
I am well aware of what is happening in some of the homes for the aged throughout Canada. It is true that there is accommodation there for them. But there is no hospital section in addition to these homes for the aged. This may not be a federal matter; it may come under the jurisdiction of the provincial health authorities. Nevertheless, that situation still exists. Often it is not possible to get some of these aged hospital cases into homes for the aged. I therefore leave that matter for the minister to consider because, in the future, we are going to have to deal with this increasing group of aged people who have become disabled through disease and who are not able to obtain accommodation in ordinary hospitals. Ordinary hospitals are jammed at the present time. The necessity for beds for acute cases is well known. Any person or any doctor who has had experience in trying to get patients into hospitals is well aware of that fact.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Another matter affecting the question of treatment is the present shortage of nurses. I am also aware that this may not be a federal matter, because the matter of trained nurses again comes within the realm of the provinces. Nevertheless, when we consider the broad picture of health across Canada, we feel that something should be done about this matter. There still exists a shortage of nurses throughout the whole of the country. It is difficult to obtain nurses for private duty. Possibly one of the reasons for that is that the nurses' hours have been cut down, something which entails the fact that we may need additional nurses. The hospitals are finding it increasingly difficult to secure a staff of nurses. This is something else in the way of difficulty being encountered by them, in addition to the financial troubles they are undergoing.
When I mention financial troubles, that brings to mind the question of the difficulty that some of these hospitals have in financing treatment for their people, both in private rooms and in wards. The cost of hospital maintenance now brings about a situation in which hospital executives find it extremely difficult to run the hospitals and to balance their accounts at the end of the year. The average hospital is run at a loss. That is something that is giving a great deal of worry to some of these people who are trying to carry on accommodation in hospitals throughout the country.
If, in addition to building, we could further the interests of the hospitals with additional money in some way, either through the provinces or through the federal department, a good deal of this trouble could be avoided. That is something that is not going to be easy to do. The unfortunate thing is that, with rising costs and with the trouble encountered in maintaining a hospital, the cost of hospital accommodation is being reflected on the patients, from those in the public wards to those in the private wards. The situation now is that it is difficult for the average person to pay for hospital accommodation. In the last few months I consulted the treasurers of some hospitals with regard to their difficulties, and I found out something that was amazing, namely that many of these hospitals would have further financial trouble if it were not for the fact that so many cases are coming in on prepaid medical plans. They are coming in on commercial plans, through organizations like the Blue Cross, and industrial health insurance; and the ordinary commercial insurance policy that we buy is now becoming fairly popular. But there is at the present time a great need that the policies which these people buy should be clarified. The people do not always look at the small

Supply-Health and Welfare print. Sometimes you have the picture of a man coming in and saying: My wife was in the hospital for a certain length of time. I thought that our insurance entirely covered this matter but I find, written in in small print at the bottom of the policy, and to which I paid no attention when I bought it, the proviso that this policy does not cover the type of disease from which my wife suffered.
Another matter which comes to my mind is the old question of research. There are still some diseases for which a cure, if we could find one, would be a boon to civilization. I refer to such diseases as cancer, poliomyelitis, multiple sclerosis, certain heart conditions and, of course, the increasing number of mental cases throughout the country. I have mentioned this matter before, and there is no doubt that the situation still exists. I refer to the fact that mental cases are increasing faster than the civilian population; or you might regard it in another way, namely in comparison with other types of cases which are admitted to hospitals as acute and chronic cases. There is a further difficulty in this matter; it has to do with the question of accommodation for people who are suffering from mental disease. There is again a great shortage of beds for patients of this type who usually require a long period of hospitalization. This is also something we shall have to deal with in the future. I mentioned first the question of these people who are going to suffer from the increasing diseases of old age. The other thing that I point out is what I have just mentioned, namely the increasing number of mental cases. We have been able to deal with the diseases of short duration, for which we have found an answer; but there is only one answer to the problem of mental disease and also those other diseases which I mentioned, and that is research. I have advocated money for research so that we might, in conjunction with other nations, find an answer to these problems. But there is much that could be done.
I was and am interested in the program put on by the Ontario government in the treatment of people who are suffering from poliomyelitis or infantile paralysis. Every case in Ontario is sent to a selected group of hospitals. The Ontario government pays the full cost of all the treatment for poliomyelitis sufferers, and owing to the fact that they are grouped together, and that the treatment is available, many cures have come to light which otherwise would not have happened had the patient been a patient at home, and probably he would have ended up a hopeless cripple. It is simply amazing what has been done under this program. While I am not


aware of what is happening in some of the other provinces in the dominion, I would suggest, sir, that if, this treatment could be furthered in any way, because of the results which have been obtained in Ontario, we should see that every poliomyelitis patient gets into one of the selected hospitals where the treatment is thoroughly understood. Although we have not an answer to the disease, the treatment could be made available to those patients.
Multiple sclerosis still exists as a problem. In a speech I made in the house during the short session last fall I mentioned that I had letters from three people scattered across my own constituency suffering from multiple sclerosis. They have spent all their money trying to get cured. They wrote asking if there was some place where a treatment could be continued or where they could be cared for. It is rather sad, sir, to see young people who are hopeless cripples, without very much to look forward to in life, trying to find some place where they can be accommodated. As I said before, it is difficult to accommodate long chronic cases in hospitals where beds are urgently demanded for acute cases.
The matter of treatment for certain cardiovascular conditions is brought to our minds every day or so, and if we could find an answer to the condition where prominent men in middle life are dropping out rapidly through coronary thrombosis attacks we would have gone a long way to solving something else which is becoming all too common. I do not know whether we have better conditions so far as diagnosis is concerned, or whether the advent of the electrocardiographs have brought to light more cases than we had before, but it does seem to me that there are more cases than formerly existed. Therefore if we could find an answer to that problem, whether it exists in our way of life, whether it has something to do with diet,-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Or age of the population.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Or ageing population.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Or of the age of the population.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are doing that. I see the item in the national health program under the research grant.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I know there is a certain amount being granted for this purpose, but my policy in regard to some of these things would be even more research. I have always backed the minister on any money that is spent for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
So that my remarks may
perhaps get out where I want them to get out, may I say that I thank my hon. friend for what he has said. We have given very considerable amounts for research in the field of mental illness. There are still available in the department funds for this purpose which we have been urging certain bodies to use-I will not say where but my hon. friend I think knows where-and I wish that it were possible for some of these agencies to take advantage of these funds in addition to what has already been done in this very important field.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I hope that the minister is able to get this thing working. I know the difficulties under which he labours, because up to this time there has not been a tendency to do research work on mental cases. I again bring to the attention of the minister the fact that last spring and the spring before we had these completely disabled people approach us for some help. It is really pitiable every year when they come here. They are in wheel chairs. Some of them are disabled beyond any possibility
Supply-Health and Welfare of doing anything that would help them to earn a living. I again suggest that in considering these estimates-I think every hon. member is in agreement-these people be admitted to the welfare group because we shall have to do something for them. We have passed a resolution to do something for the older people. Following that was a resolution to help the blind. We cannot forget the plea of these people who came before us at the time that the social security committee was sitting, asking that something be done for them.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I again lay emphasis on two major things so far as treatment in this country is concerned. First, let us do all the research work that we can do so far as the laboratories and the research workers of this country are concerned, and try to find an answer to some of these diseases for which we have no answer at the present time, and which seem to be growing with the increasing population of this country. Again I make a plea that consideration be given to some form of hospitals for the aged in this country where these people who are suffering from the chronic diseases of old age may get accommodation and treatment. This group is constantly growing and is going to become a problem- something we cannot very well avoid, because we have found the answer to other acute diseases and, with a population living longer, this group is becoming steadily larger. It is needless to point out that some of these chronic heart cases and the cancer cases for a year or two need nursing. They need something more than is given to them in homes for the aged. This is a group somewhere in between those who would go to hospitals for acute cases and those who would go to homes for the aged. In some way we must make arrangements whereby we can take care of these people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am sure that on this occasion I can speak for members in all sections of the house when I say that we always listen with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark when he speaks on matters relating to health, a field in which he is well qualified.
I think, too, that when he spoke about the urgent needs of our incurables and invalids, those in the condition of some who have visited us from time to time, he was likewise expressing the views of members in all parts of the house. I want to add once again my wholehearted support to the plea the hon. member for Lanark has just made, that the government refrain from delaying action with respect to this group of people. I am reminded again of the discussions in the committee on old age security which met last

Supply-Health and Welfare year. There, despite the fact that it was outside our terms of reference, on several occasions we found ourselves confronted with the problem of invalids and incurables; and it was the feeling of members of that committee that something should be done for them.
From time to time we have had discussions in the house on a motion brought in perennially by the hon. member for Terrebonne. I trust he will continue to present his motion to the house. Unfortunately that motion has never come to a vote, so that we have not been able to test the opinion of the house. I am sure if there were a free vote on it the motion would carry. I hope the government will recognize that fact and that it will not be long before there are pensions or other appropriate provisions for those unfortunate Canadians whom we refer to as invalids and incurables.
The phase of the work of the department to which I should like to address myself, in the main, is in fact the subject dealt with in the opening words of the hon. member for Lanark. Indeed, although I like to see things going along peacefully for the most part, I was rather glad to note that he provoked a bit of a squabble at the beginning of his speech. I was interested to hear him read certain comments from the press, which prompted the hon. member for Coast-Capilano to get in his nickel's worth, and which prompted the Minister of National Health and Welfare to reply as well.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You would not want to discuss this item when it comes up, would you? You could have a discussion then.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think I would rather discuss it now, just as the hon. member for Lanark discussed it now. I was just going to point out that what has disturbed me most in the last few years has been the indifference shown to this question of health insurance. Therefore I was glad to see a bit of a fight about it today, and I hope there will be more squabbles of that nature, even if they are political, if only we can get some attention paid to this important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You know there is no indifference, and it is not fair to create that impression.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Oh, Mr. Chairman, not only do I know that there is indifference to it, but I noted on Saturday, May 5, in Arthur Blakely's Ottawa-Day-By-Day column appearing daily in the Montreal Gazette, this short paragraph:
Health insurance which once held a high priority in the federal government's plans, may be a Korean

casualty. Old age pensions proposals are going ahead, but health insurance studies have been slowed down or discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Blakely is a very estimable and fine man, but he does not have his finger on everything. That statement is inaccurate, and no one knows it more than the hon. member who is just speaking.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When all these members
get through saying "hear, hear" may I remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare that I have been trying for several years in the discussion on his estimates to get him to give us some evidence of the work he says is being done with respect to health insurance studies. When we get down to the item of which he speaks-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When we get down to the
item; let us get down to it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister used to interrupt us like this three or four years ago, but I thought he was getting over that habit and was letting us make our own speeches. The fact of the matter is that the minister is annoyed by these references to the indifference of his department to health insurance studies. That simply proves to me that nothing is being done about this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The by-election will be over
on Monday.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The by-election will be over on Monday.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Now, you know, Mr. Chairman, it is a good thing we have by-elections. I take it that some members in the committee were glad that the by-election in Winnipeg South Centre took me out of the house for a couple of days-and some members are sorry I did not stay longer. What is good about these by-elections is that they-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Order. We are not discussing by-elections.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am not discussing them at all. I am just pointing out that contests of that kind result in discussions on issues such as health insurance which, normally, the government tries to ignore. The hon. member for Lanark read a report from the Toronto Telegram telling us that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in the constituency of Waterloo South is telling the people down there that we are going to have a program of national health insurance. Well, I listened the other night in Winnipeg to an address over the radio by the Minister of National Health and Welfare-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: A good speech, wasn't it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Oh, I would have known whose speech it was even had it not been announced as the minister's speech, and even had it not been in his voice. I would have known from the way in which he overstated things just exactly who it was. But I did not hear him announce out in the constituency of Winnipeg South Centre that there was going to be a program of national health insurance. Instead, we get that in Waterloo South from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
I am glad to have all these interjections.
I hope they reach Hansard. The reason I am pleased is that any squabble we have about this matter draws attention to it. I hope the result of it will be some action at an early date.
I do not need to speak at length on this matter, for I was provoked into making a speech on it last night, because of the terms of an answer given by the Prime Minister to a question asked yesterday when the orders of the day were called. I was certainly disturbed by the readiness with which the Prime Minister seemed to accept the idea that health insurance could be taken over and administered by the Canadian Medical Association.
I have the greatest respect and the highest regard for the medical profession. As a matter of fact I would not be here today were it not for the life-saving abilities of some of its members. But when it comes to administering health insurance I submit, as I suggested last night, that the program to which the Liberal party has already committed itself is the correct one, and that it should be handled in the name of the people of Canada by their government.
Now that we are taking forward steps in the field of old age security legislation, I feel that the most significant gap in our social security legislation is in this field of health insurance. Indeed I have in my hand a copy of a little pamphlet that was put out by the wartime information board during the war. This one was issued on November 15, 1944, and is one of a series designed primarily for the troops overseas so that they might know what was going on back home. The name of the series was "Canadian Affairs" and the title of this one is, "Canada plans security". In this very excellent summary of what was being done in this country I find this paragraph:
What about sickness? There are still gaps in our social security program. Chief among these concerns the question of illness. When sickness strikes, it strikes with a two-edged sword. Not only does the workman lose his pay during the period he is away from work-worse than that, he has to bear
Supply-Health and Welfare the crushing blow of medical, hospital, and other expenses, running sometimes into hundreds of dollars.
Having discussed the proposals for various social security measures which were being put forward at that time, the pamphlet had this to say:
Lost wages. There still remains the problem of loss of income due to sickness. Unemployment insurance only covers the worker who has lost a job and is still available for employment. If you are sick, you aren't available for employment-so you don't get unemployment insurance. Once health insurance is finally put into operation, it probably won't be long until the Unemployment Insurance Act is amended to provide for payment of benefits during the period of a workman's illness.
If that happens then a worker off for sickness would get unemployment insurance sickness benefit to make up for lost wages and would have his medical and hospital expenses met out of the health insurance fund-to which he has been contributing.
I read those excerpts from pamphlets put out, as I say, by the wartime information board during the years of the war just to indicate that the ideas that some of us proclaim are not so strange after all. That is precisely in line with what we have been saying from this corner of the house for a long time, namely, that health insurance is the most serious gap in our social security program and that an adequate healtht insurance plan requires at least three things.
It requires the provision of sufficient services, including hospitals, clinics, doctors, and everything that is needed to take care of the health of our people. Second, it requires a plan to enable the people to get those services; in other words, a plan that will pay for them. There is no point to having the best hospitals and the best doctors available if our people cannot avail themselves of their services without mortgaging the rest of their lives.
The third thing we need, and this is underlined in the quotations I have just read from this interesting pamphlet, is something in the nature of sickness benefits. When the wage earner is off sick it is not enough that there is a good hospital to go to or a fine doctor to attend him; it is not enough that his hospital bills are paid; there is also the problem of lost income. I thoroughly agree with the position taken in this Canadian Affairs pamphlet that something must be done along that line.
I know that this is getting to be an, old song with me, but I am going to repeat it and probably will continue doing so until we get some action along this line. What I would like to see would be the government bring in legislation in the field of health insurance. I would like to see the government come through with the kind of money that was talked about in 1945 when the

Supply-Health and Welfare federal government made proposals to the provinces for expenditures totalling $150 million a year on health services. The health grants program which was started in 1948 has entailed an annual expenditure in the order of $30 million, which is considerably less than $150 million suggested at the dominion-provincial conference in 1945.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is twice as much as the grants program proposed in 1945.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The total program proposed in 1945 called for an expenditure by the federal government of $150 million. Thirty million is not twice $150 million, it is only one-fifth.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants to confuse it, I cannot help it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If anybody is trying to confuse I suggest it is the minister when he says that $30 million is twice $150 million. The federal government is spending only $30 million.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Only $30 million?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

I submit that there is no field in which we could invest money more effectively or more usefully than in the field of national health. Before I was interrupted two or three times, I was going to say about six or seven minutes ago that my first choice would be for the government to bring in without delay legislation covering the field of health insurance, including all three of the major points in a health insurance program to which I referred a few moments ago.

If the government is going to be as slow as it usually is in these matters; if the government is going to continue to require to be prodded, despite the statement of the minister this morning that the government does not have to be prodded in these matters-we could not help but laugh at that-I suggest that the second best method to get this ball rolling is to set up a special committee on health insurance similar to the committee that was set up last year on old age security.
If the minister wants to pick up Hansard of early 1950 he can find in the debate on the motion to set up that committee that I objected to it. I doubted whether it was a good move, and I admit that readily. I had strong ideas as to what were the real motives behind the motion. But I admit now that that committee did an excellent job. Every member of the committee paid close attention to the task before him. We did a lot of research and we came out with a most useful and acceptable report. That report represents a milestone in our progress along this road. It represents a step along the way, although it must be remembered- that there are other steps to be taken.
I am convinced that a similar committee on health insurance-if you like, it can be composed of the same personnel-could do an excellent piece of work in studying this question. I am satisfied -that it would make recommendations which might likewise be another milestone in this field. I was disappointed that the Minister of National Health and Welfare found it possible on two occasions during -this session to say "No" to my request that such a committee be set up. I was disappointed also that yesterday the Prime Minister brushed aside that question. I still make -the plea and I hope the government will consider it between now and the October session. If there are any good reasons-and I cannot see any-why we should not have such a committee at that session at least I hope they will consider setting up such a special committee at the regular session of 1952. I say again that I agree with the views expressed in this Canadian Affairs pamphlet that the most significant gap in our social security program concerns the question of illness and I hope that we will soon start to take some worth-while steps in the field of health insurance, as part of an over-all social security program.

Mr. Chairman, there are two points with which I wish to deal briefly. The first is hospitalization. There seems to be some difficulty in most parts of Canada in stabilizing the cost of hospital services. In one or two provinces this issue is very

serious. To those who find this problem a bit perplexing I would suggest that they study the Alberta hospitalization plan. The purpose of Alberta's provincial hospitalization plan is to bring hospital services within the average citizen's ability to pay for them. This is done by distributing the total cost between the province, the municipalities and the patients. The plan comes into operation when the municipal council has passed the necessary bylaw and signed the prescribed agreement with an approved hospital or hospitals. I have in my .hand a copy of "Within Our Borders", for February, 1951, and I should like to quote briefly therefrom with respect to Alberta's hospitalization plan. It reads as follows:
Hospitals are graded according to their size, type of equipment, number of doctors and nurses, and other considerations. What is called "basic ward rate" ranges from $5.50 per day in a class A hospital to $4.25 per day in a class E hospital. Ordinarily the patient would have to pay the whole amount plus extras, but under the provincial plan he or she pays only $1 per day plus extras. The balance, which in a class A hospital would be $4.50 per day, is paid by the municipal authority with whom the agreement has been signed, and they in turn are reimbursed one-half of this amount from the provincial treasury.
Some of the highlights of the provincial hospitalization plan are worth emphasizing, and I should like to enumerate some of these points. Quoting from the same publication, they are:
1.	Hospitalization grants are paid to any municipality on condition that the local council enter into an agreement with an approved hospital to provide standard ward accommodation at $1 per day for their ratepayers.
2.	This deterrent charge ensures hospitalization to the people of Alberta at a price which the great majority can afford, while at the same time it guards against an excessive demand for hospitalization which usually accompanies so-called free hospitalization.
3.	The plan does not apply to maternity cases, pensioners, indigent patients or those coming under the Workmen's Compensation Act because hospitalization for these is provided under other legislation.
4.	All conditions requiring treatment in hospital are covered for as long as may be necessary.
5.	Pre-existing conditions are not excluded from hospital treatment.
6.	Admission to hospital for diagnostic services is covered under the plan.
7.	Patients referred to other hospitals by their local physicians and emergency admissions to other hospitals are provided for.
8.	Hospital taxes in the municipalities are based on real property values, thus apportioning the share of the municipality in an equitable manner.
9.	Administration of the provincial plan is left mainly with local authorities, and as a result hospitals are free from bureaucratic control.
It is thus that the province of Alberta is solving the problem of hospitalization for its residents. There is one other matter that I should like to deal with briefly. In looking over the estimates we find grants of various amounts for many worthy causes.
Supply-Health and Welfare I would suggest that the minister could take an additional step in the progress of health services by providing a grant to be used for further development and research in chiropractic. There is great need for chiropractic service in the armed forces. Under the government rehabilitation scheme veterans tuition and living expenses were paid for a considerable number of men who chose chiropractic as a career. It takes a considerable amount of money to finance a student through a four-year course. Since the government already has a considerable investment in the training of these men, and since the Canadian Legion has requested chiropractic service, it seems logical that this service should be made available to those members of the armed forces who desire such service.
The usual answer is that such services are already provided for the armed forces. When this statement is made the reference is to physiotherapy, massage, and so on. Physiotherapists have their place and are doing good work, but physiotherapy is not a part of chiropractic. Chiropractic is not a duplication of any other method of health service. It is definitely different and therefore does have something to offer which is not a duplication of the service rendered by any other type of health service. I want to make it abundantly clear that I am not trying to minimize the service rendered by medicine or any other branch of the healing profession. My point is that we are living in a day of specialization, and since chiropractic does have an exclusive approach in rendering health services I claim that we should make the fullest use of that service.
For example, if one has a broken arm one certainly would not go to see a dentist. If a patient has an inflamed appendix which is about ready to rupture it would be useless to go to see a chiropractor. By the same method of reasoning if a patient has a subluxated vertebra which is interfering with the normal flow of life energy to a particular organ or tissue of the body, it is also reasonable to say that all the drugs and tonics on the North American continent would not release that subluxation. To illustrate my point further, I should like to use some fundamental philosophy. There are only three things in the world. Those three things are intelligence, force and matter. If we consider the world and everything in it we will find that everything is composed of these three elements. Likewise we have three types of health services to correspond with the three elements of universe. If we were to take all the healing professions and list them we would find that they would come under the three headings

Christian Science, of course, believes that you can control matter through mind. This may or may not be so; I am not prepared to argue the point this afternoon. As far as psychiatry, psychology and psychosomatic medicine are concerned, they are all doing very good work. They deal entirely with our educated mind, which is only a part of our innate mind. They are very necessary in our healing profession.
So far we have listed those healing arts which come under intelligence and matter. This leaves only one other heading, according to the triune of life; that would be force or energy. Under this heading we would find only one healing profession listed; that is chiropractic. That is the only healing profession which deals with the link between intelligence and matter. It may be argued that other branches of healing also deal with the transmission of energy from intelligence to matter. They say energy can


be stimulated by massage, by tonics and things of that kind, which is partly true. I might use the example of a small stream. If you operate a paddle in that stream naturally the water will run faster, but when you stop paddling the water will settle down to its normal flow again.
The first principle of chiropractic is that there is a universal intelligence which governs the universe and everything in it. It is this universal intelligence that keeps the earth from bumping into the moon, that makes the grass' grow green every year instead of blue one year and yellow the next year. We as human beings have an inborn intelligence which is part of this universal intelligence. It is this innate intelligence which makes our body live, which keeps our body temperature constant at 98-6 degrees without any effort on the part of our educated mind, that keeps our heart beating 72 times a minute whether we are awake or asleep. It is this innate intelligence which secretes the gastric juices when we smell a beefsteak and so on. It is this innate intelligence that makes the difference between a living body and dead body. If it were possible to take a dead body and a live body and put them in two test tubes and make an analysis, you would find they would both boil down to about 95 cents' worth of chemicals. Therefore the only difference between the two is this innate intelligence. This innate intelligence is the only difference between life and death. So to have 100 per cent health one must have 100 per cent intelligence, 100 per cent energy or force, and 100 per cent matter.
Innate intelligence operates through the brain, which generates energy and sends it down the spinal cord and out through the millions of nerves which radiate to every organ, gland and tissue in the body. Without these nerve impulses or energy which flow from the brain to the heart, the heart could not pump blood, glands could not function, muscles could not move. Nerve impulses are the life force that drives the intricate machinery of the human body. Interference with the flow of this life force means disease. Since energy flows from the brain through the nerves to the organs, glands, tissues and so on, the logical place to look for interference would be along the nerve lines. A quick glance at the nervous anatomy will show that the most likely place to find interference or subluxations would be as the nerve leaves the spinal column.
The chiropractor is trained to locate and remove these subluxations. That is done by means of such instruments as the neurocalo-meter, microdynameter, the X-ray and so on. To substantiate the claims I have made I would like to refer briefly to an analysis of

2,975 cases taken from the files of workmen's compensation bureaux. In making this survey the research committee was careful to include all back strains whether cared for by a chiropractor or by a doctor of medicine. The cases in the medical-hospitalized- category were by no means more serious than those handled by chiropractic without benefit of hospitalization. Only low back cases involving strains and sprains were included. Surgical cases, cases resulting from high level falls, crushing injuries, and the like were not included. Although only lower back cases were considered in the survey, it should be noted that chiropractic is not confined to this type of case. Indeed, many who have gone to the chiropractor because of a strain or sprain in the lower back have been relieved of other long-standing chronic conditions at the same time, many of which were considered incurable by other healing methods. In a survey made by the research committee among chiropractors in the field it was discovered that 34-5 per cent of those cases having chronic ailments had a history of some accident which was very probably responsible for the nerve pressure which was interfering with normal functions. These cases responded to chiropractic care as well as those with more acute conditions.
The figures included in this study were compiled from workmen's compensation files of Iowa (February, 1946, to February, 1948), Arkansas (1945 to 1948), and Kentucky (1940 to 1949). Mr. Chairman, I want to congratulate those who have taken part in this debate, and more particularly my good friend the hon. member for Lanark for his well-known interest in the sick and the afflicted. I will not deal with the physiology Mr. Beyerstein.]
of life or try to tell why we click. I did not know before that my medical confreres were so inefficient.
This is only the second time that I have chosen to enter the debate since moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Many subjects have been before hon. members to which I might have made some contribution, but I preferred to leave it to the experts. I do not pretend to be an expert on health measures, but by reason of practising medicine and surgery for thirty years, I think I may reasonably be expected to know something of what goes on in the health department.
I would suggest, first of all, that the department of health might well start at home and give members of this house some lessons in health measures. We all become prisoners to a system whereby we are pent up in this house from nine o'clock or ten o'clock in the morning until eleven o'clock at night. We should all have some leisure time in the evening for reading and for preparing work for the following day. I think it was the hon. member for Peel who said that the hours were inhuman. Certainly our system is not compatible with any rules of health with which I am familiar. We all should commend the Prime Minister, the Leader of the official Opposition and the leaders of the other opposition groups in their agreement to find ways and means in future to expedite the work in this House of Commons. I should also like to commend Mr. Speaker for his interest in the need for improvement of the acoustics of this chamber. Since I have been here many a good speech has been dissipated into the upper realms of space as you could not hear it. That is because our voices lack the volume and the quality necessary in a chamber of this size. The spoken word certainly leaves a more lasting impression; and when this work is finished, the use of Hansard in this house at least should be relegated to those who are engaged in research in the realm of words in order to harass and to embarrass their authors.
I should like to commend the minister and the personnel of his department for the fine work they are doing for the people of Canada generally. To my mind health matters transcend party politics, as well they should. Our only differences should be in the amount and degree of health services provided. A critical scrutiny of the estimates should always be welcome so that we can get the most for the health dollar. I will not attempt to enumerate or describe the recent advances in medicine and surgery-I think the hon. member for Lanark described some of these.
I will say, however, that many of the effective

new drugs are very expensive and add greatly to the cost of medical care. I would think that the main purpose of the health department should be to see that these new scientific discoveries and treatments are made available to all our people, and to help maintain our health standards at a high level.
In moving the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I referred to the interest I had in the national health program announced in May, 1948. At that time I enumerated some of the main features. The various federal and provincial surveys now being conducted, to my mind, will supply some of the information necessary to evolve a national health scheme of contributory health insurance.
In talking about such a scheme I fully realize that the inauguration and payment of universal old age pensions to those 70 and over, and 50 per cent to those between 65 and 70 will be inflationary, and will have a very considerable impact on our economy.
I realize also that health matters, and certainly, more particularly those that apply to patients treated in our general hospitals in the provinces, are under provincial jurisdiction.
I want to thank the Prime Minister for the compliment he paid to my profession here yesterday. I think the medical profession in Canada realizes its responsibilities fully. According to the members of their executive they want to give our people the best possible prepaid medical care. The trans-Canada medical services is really a consolidation of the seven provincial medical services already in existence. They state that they believe they can provide a better and more economical service than can be done by the government when it is government run. I believe this to be the case, because I know that the medical associations have been studying medical economics for some time.
I hear some criticism of the scheme because it is being run by doctors. Some people also say that doctors are poor businessmen. That may be so, but I think they can run a good scheme. I think the system should be on the fee-for-service basis, for we want to maintain the basic freedoms and a high standard of medical services in Canada. In any event, I think it should be studied, and I am certainly in favour of the most economical system. The trouble with the scheme at the present time is that the membership is limited. You can become a member only if you belong to a group. Self-employed persons and individuals cannot join. I feel that these details will be corrected in time.
This scheme is much more ambitious than the one I had the temerity to propose last 80709-283j
Supply-Health and Welfare January. I talked about a contributory plan for the major medical expenses. This plan is much more inclusive and should receive the study of all members of this government, because expenses incidental to sickness are the last major element left in the feeling of insecurity of our people.
In suggesting some type of contributory health insurance in January I had in mind that many schemes were in force, but they all had some drawbacks, and I will give these quickly, and that will be all.
(1)	For the most part they are sold to groups, and as such are not easily available to a large majority of our people.
(2)	Most of them have limitations as to the amount of benefits and the length of time they may be received.

speechtext: The age of sickness.

Yes.
(3)	They do not present a true picture of the cost of medical services, because those admitted are reasonably healthy, since they are engaged in production.
(4)	Many schemes terminate at the time of, or soon after, the termination of employment. I think this is important.
(5)	There is no uniformity of coverage. This can militate against the labouring man. I have known men to remain in one place of employment instead of taking more preferable employment because of the better medical and hospital coverage where they are.
(6)	I have been told by employers, for instance, that they would not hire men over 50, and prefer not to hire men older than 40, because of the higher premium for medical and insurance coverage necessary for a higher average age group. I am convinced that we should encourage the employment of the older age group. Most people are much happier and healthier when they are employed. Discontent, sickness and misery are often early manifestations of the idleness of retirement. We would be making a fatal mistake to have all our taxation fall on too narrow or contracted an age group of our people. It would bog down our economy. We should rather always try to broaden that age base for a better economy and for happier Canadians.

When we got to discussing the matter, partly through questions on the orders of the day, and I believe at one time on supplementary estimates, I made it clear that the use of the word "dyed" did not imply that any unhealthy elements were being put into bread, but rather that purchasers of bread were being deceived. The deception lies in the fact that most people who buy brown bread think they are getting whole wheat bread. I understand that when a loaf of brown bread is wrapped, if it is labelled "Canada approved" it has to have a certain content of whole wheat flour. But if the loaf of brown bread is not so labelled there are no provisions in the Food and Drugs Act requiring that there be any particular content of whole wheat flour.
On one of the occasions when this matter was under discussion the minister was good enough to let me know that the matter was being considered. What progress is being made in connection with the hospital at Norway House? Although it is not in my constituency, I am interested in it. How many new hospital stations have been built in the north country since the last estimates were before us?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I know the hon. member knows a good deal about Norway House. We have an item of $500,000 in the estimates for the construction of a fifty-bed hospital at Norway House. The hon. member may be assured, as I have assured him privately, that we are anxious to see the construction there as quickly as possible. The hospital at that point is very old, and we would have replaced it earlier but for the fact that our program of hospital construction envisaged building new units in places where there were no units at all. We have reached the point now where we have met that aspect of our program and, as I have indicated, we are now able to give attention to such things as Norway House.
The hon. member has asked for a general picture of the progress made. As he knows, in addition to our 18 hospitals-those at Qu'Appelle, at Nanaimo, at Coqualeetza and the Charles Camsell hospital are the major ones-we have 29 nursing stations and 49 health centres. We are making a real inroad into this problem of Indian health, one of which the people of Canada have every reason to be proud. This is largely due to the fact that we have been able to hospitalize t.b. patients among Indians, whose incidence of tuberculosis is so high.
As an indication of this perhaps it would be well if I were to place on record a brief statistical review with respect to the tuberculosis death rate in our country. This death rate has dropped 31 per cent in four years. For each one hundred thousand of population

the Indian t.b. rate in 1946 was 579-1; in 1947,549-8; 1948, 480-1; and 1949, the last year for which the figures are available, 399-6. This shows the tremendous reduction in the incidence of this disease, and this reduction is largely attributable to the increase of hospital service being provided from one end of the country to the other.
Among the white population the incidence of deaths from t.b. per one hundred thousand population was: in 1946, 41-9; 1947, 38-2; 1948, 32-4; and 1949, 26-7. The hon. member will see that the reduction in the t.b. rate among Indians is not as great as among the white population. That is due largely to the fact that the campaign against tuberculosis among the white population was begun at the close of the first great war, and took effect at the two levels of government. A real attack was made on the disease. It is only within the last short space of time, less than a decade, that we have accelerated the campaign against t.b. among the Indians. Last year, for instance, out of the population of 133,000 Indians we X-rayed almost 72,000. That indicates the extent of the service being provided, and is in great measure responsible for the showing I am able to report.

Is it the intention of the department to build more nursing stations? Are they a big help in getting people to other hospitals? What progress will be made at Norway House this summer, so' far as the hospital is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is hoped that we will make good progress this summer. It is our objective to make considerable progress before the autumn.
Are more nursing stations to be established in the far north?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes; that is part of our campaign, to the extent of our ability to provide personnel and the necessary funds.

The minister has indicated considerable progress in the last three or four years in looking after the health of Indians. That is satisfactory to everyone in Canada who has had any experience with the native population. I was somewhat disturbed in looking over the details of the estimates to see that the number of people on the staff in the Indian affairs branch has been reduced by thirty-four.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
They were thirty-four positions that had not been filled, junior positions having nothing to do with the health services work.

I was hopeful that that was not an indication that the work was slackening off, so far as the health of Indians was concerned.

While the minister's figures indicated that there has been an improvement from 579-1 per thousand in 1946 to 399-6 in 1949, nevertheless the rate is very high-about fifteen times as high as that among the white population. So long as we have a rate among the Indians fifteen times as high as that among the white population it indicates that a great deal more must be done in trying to stamp out this plague among the native population. The minister said that about 72,000 Indians have now been X-rayed. I should like to ask what arrangements have been made or what is being done in the current year to have the remaining Indians X-rayed for tjb.?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We are going ahead with our mobile clinics and we have provided additional equipment in areas where it was not in existence. We are making arrangements in some provinces for X-rays by local hospital units and by local practising physicians. Our aim is to have every available Indian in Canada X-rayed before the end of 1953. I have asked my officials why that cannot be done by the end of 1952, but I am told that that is the abjective toward which we must work. That does not mean that it is going to be easily reached, but my hon. friend may be sure that we intend to pursue this with the vigour which I think he will admit has characterized the activities to date of the Indian health division.

I am glad the department is pressing ahead with this, but after all 72,000 is just about half the Indians in Canada. It seems to me that more rapid progress could have been made. Large numbers of these Indians must be in inhabited areas which are fairly accessible, and it would seem that a little more intensive work would get things done much more rapidly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
