Why this decrease of twelve in the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
We did not need them last
year.

There must have been an
overestimate to begin with when the hospital is filled to capacity.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
There was. You cannot
estimate things exactly.

A considerable number of
doctors, nurses, cleaners, helpers, ward aides and housemaids are covered by this item. Could the minister state how many Indians are employed in these positions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I cannot give the exact
number, but we are endeavouring in the main to employ Indians in certain kinds of posts. Obviously there are posts where that cannot be done. We do not succeed fully, but to the extent that it is possible, that is our objective.

Can the minister give an
estimate of how many Indians are employed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Offhand I cannot, but I
will provide the information before the estimates are over.

I ask that question because in the past, in both the health branch and the Indian Affairs branch, there have not been anything like the number of Indians employed that could have been employed or should be employed. That is a situation which I hope will be corrected and that is why I am anxious to get the figures.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I agree fully with the hon.
member.

There is an item of
$4,730,000 covering hospital, doctors' and


other professional and special fees. Apparently this is in addition to the considerable number of doctors and other people who are regular or part-time employees of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
This item is required to pay
the accounts of more than 700 hospitals and 800 doctors, dentists, nurses and other persons providing treatment or other care and attention to sick Indians and Eskimos. The increase is due to the fact that expenditures in the last six months of 1950-51 amounted to $2,300,000 and it is anticipated that this rate of expenditure at least will continue for this year. As my hon. friend knows, the main job of looking after Indian help is not done here at the centre where we have a relatively small administrative personnel. It is done by our full-time personnel in the hospitals and nursing units throughout the country, and in addition we rely upon assistance in many hundreds of localities, as I have indicated, from doctors who work on a fee per person basis in treating Indians.

You have listed 54 parttime physicians, in addition to some 50 odd regular medical officers. Then there is this other large item for doctors' and other professional and special fees. I assume that those are fees to doctors who are not on the part-time staff?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is right.

And dental and hospital
fees for Indians treated in hospitals apart from the Indian Affairs hospitals?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I might tell my hon. friend
that many hospitals are not satisfied with our payments. Some of them feel that the per diem rate is not sufficient and we are having controversy over that matter. I am trying to meet it within the budget at my disposal. If it were not for that, I am afraid the amount would be considerably larger.
I do not want to leave the impression in the mind of the minister or anyone else that I am complaining about the amount. I was merely trying to find out what the explanation was.

During the spring many of us had the opportunity of making a trip to Churchill and visiting the hospital there and I feel the time has come when an opposition member should advocate an additional expenditure. I was much impressed with the work being done in the army hospital there where they were trying to treat Eskimos and Indians. I feel that that hospital should be rebuilt and I would advocate some arrangement being made between the Department of

National Health and Welfare and the Department of National Defence to provide new hospital accommodation. A survey of the number of Indians and Eskimos in the vicinity would probably show that a combined operation could be carried on and it might be that a wing could be erected or a new hospital provided for these people.
I think all hon. members who visited there must realize that a new hospital would be desirable, not only for the defence forces stationed there but for the many Indians and Eskimos. Therefore you have the peculiar thing of an opposition member advocating expenditure, but I never feel it should be considered an expense. I feel that it would be money well expended and would bring returns.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend was kind
enough to mention that to me some time ago, and we are looking into it. As he knows, many of the existing hospitals we have are institutions that were used by the armed forces during the war which we were able to get for a reasonable consideration, and which now form an important part of our hospital chain throughout the country.

I wish to take a moment to say a few words on this item of operation and maintenance of Indian and Eskimo health services. I want to take this opportunity to pay a tribute to the minister and lhis staff for the increased medical care and hospitalization that our Indian population is now getting. Last winter I had the opportunity of going through the Indian hospital located at the airport at North Battleford. I was escorted through the institution under the guidance of Dr. Head, the capable superintendent in charge. I was shown up-to-date equipment and was escorted through the various wards. I should like to mention the matron, Miss J. M. Morton, R.N., a 1936 graduate of the Regina general hospital. She also served overseas as nurse lieutenant for some two and a half years during the last war, and after serving at the Prince Rupert Indian hospital came to North Battle-ford some two years ago.
I was informed that more than 1,400 patients have passed through the hospital since its inception. Of this number some 145 were major surgical cases. There were 125 babies delivered during this period including one set of twins, and also 1,000 out patients were treated. Before taking my seat I should like to mention the work and skill of one of the nurses working under Nurse Morton. I wish to refer to Martha Soonias who was born on the Red Pheasant reserve, educated at Saskatoon and later took a mothercraft course in Toronto. After a post-graduate course in New Zealand, where
Supply-Health and Welfare she qualified as a registered midwife, she served for a time on the staff of St. Helen's hospital, Wellington, New Zealand. She returned to Canada in January, 1948, and joined the staff of the Indian hospital then being assembled there. I should just like to say that I consider that great steps forward have been taken in recent years by this department for the care and treatment of our first Canadians.

When I was making a few
remarks about tuberculosis I forgot to ask one question. To what extent do the hospitals of the department look after tubercular Indians who need hospitalization? In other words, how many tubercular Indians are there, if any, who cannot be accommodated in these hospitals?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: To the extent of our'facilities every Indian who is suffering from tuberculosis in such a way that he requires that kind of attention is either in a nursing station or in one of our own hospitals. We endeavour to keep them in the nursing stations only for the minimum period before transferring them to our own hospitals. In very many instances, notably in the province of Ontario where they have an excellent system of sanatoria, Indians are quartered in those places, but to the extent that our facilities will permit there is no Indian suffering from tuberculosis and needing hospitalization who is not getting it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Indians and Eskimos health services-
271.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and new equipment, $1,609,000.

Will the minister tell us
what hospital construction is going ahead this year? I presume if there is any it is under construction now inasmuch as we are well into the building season.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
We are providing for an addition to our hospital at Fort Qu'Appelle of some fifty beds, the construction of a modern hospital at Norway House, to which the hon. member for Selkirk has already directed my attention. We are engaged in the restoration of the fire damage at our hospital at Coqua-leetza in the riding of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, which unfortunately took place a short time ago. We are providing for the repair of the staff quarters of the Charles Camsell Indian hospital at Edmonton, which is our largest hospital having some 453 beds. Undoubtedly my hon. friend knows about it. Then we are providing for a doctors' residence at the Fisher River Indian reserve. I might say I have encountered some reluctance in securing authorization for these physicians' residences, but
4454	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare there are some cases where you simply cannot get medical help unless they are provided, and naturally so. That is the program of construction envisaged at the present time.

I take it that this is all a
matter of finishing construction which was started last year, and that there is no new construction with the possible exception of this residence.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Norway House is new.
It was not under construction last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
277. Hospital design and consulting service, $24,286.

Can the minister say how
many are employed in this division, what work they are doing, and whom they advise with respect to hospital construction, and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: There are five people engaged in that division, which I believe is a very useful one. I should like to pay a public tribute to the director of the division who was offered a job in Ottawa by the architects of Canada at a salary $3,200 more than the maximum his present position carries. In this instance, knowing all the circumstances, it was out of a sense of clear public duty that he has continued in this post. When the opportunity comes to pay tribute to public service of that type I think one should not hesitate to do so, and I have done so in this house today because he deserves it. Naturally he plays a very big part in the development of our national health program, particularly with respect to our hospital construction campaign. Over the last two and one-quarter years we have collaborated with the provincial governments in providing nearly 30,000 additional hospital beds in Canada. That is an achievement which I am sure Canada will note with the greatest measure of satisfaction. This particular officer plays a great part in assisting local bodies in the designing of hospitals, in saving them money and providing efficient operation. He is able to do so because of his exclusive experience over the last five years in hospital design work. He has a staff of five. I may say that his staff is not large enough and we have had to rely upon assistance from other departments. That we have done. I cannot speak too highly of this division.

I am very glad to hear the minister say that. I raise the point particularly because I am all in favour of the good work being done by officials of this branch.


However, the cost of hospitals is a very serious thing to the people of Canada, and in particular to the people of British Columbia. Here we have a department in Ottawa dealing with hospital design. The provincial governments have departments dealing with hospital design. Then when you come to build a hospital you have to pay an architect a percentage of the total cost.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not believe there is one provincial government that has a hospital design division.

Pardon me, they may not be termed hospital design divisions, but in British Columbia there is an architects branch which advises in the construction of schools and hospitals. Then when a local hospital board comes to build a hospital they have got to employ an architect and pay a percentage of the cost to him. Personally I should like to see the federal and provincial governments carry this right through in order to save the taxpayers money and provide supervision in construction.	.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
278. Mental health, $50,610.

Would the minister say what co-operation there is between the provincial mental health departments and the federal department? I was also going to ask the reason for the decrease in this item this year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I was going to say there is no decrease; I was thinking of the mental health grant item, on which I wanted to.say a few words, and I might as well do so right now. The decrease in this item, however, is not indicative of any lessening of our efforts to do something about mental health. It results from the fact that we have eliminated some of our public information items in the field of mental health, to the extent of about $35,000. This is part of our program of public information that was conceived some time ago, and this year we are not going ahead with some films and some literature which we and the provinces have agreed are not necessary just now. In view of what the hon. member for Lanark said in his excellent statement I want to reassure him and all hon. members that we regard this problem of mental health as one of our most serious challenges, and I think we are meeting it.
The biggest single grant we have in the national health program is for assistance in mental health. As hon. members have noted, more than 50 per cent of our hospital beds are occupied by patients who suffer from mental ill health. This is a challenge we have to face. It is not a problem peculiar to

Canada; it is true of other countries as well. The causes are perhaps controversial, but they exist. We have embarked upon a program, and I sometimes wish I had time to really go into detail and tell the house what is being done. It is not simply because I am the minister; I am sure no body of public servants in the government of Canada is engaged in greater work than the officers of my department working in this field of health, particularly in mental health control. When I think of what the national health program has done in this field alone I feel that I may have been amiss in not bringing home these great achievements.
We have moved1 from a policy of mere custodial care into actual treatment. Perhaps I misunderstood the glance of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but I assure him that is of the utmost significance. The result is that today we see people leaving our institutions who a decade ago would have been kept there for years. That is due largely to the sort of therapy which is being provided at federal expense in order to supplement the great work being done by the provincial departments of health. The training of occupational therapists is under the national health program, and1 they go into institutions in the provinces, many of which formerly could not afford them. The results are phenomenal. But we are not stopping at that; we are engaged in a program of prevention. We now have thirty-nine mental health clinics in Canada as a result of this program, by which we hope to relieve many people of the necessity of going into mental institutions, by getting them in the earliest stages and treating them in their local communities. One such clinic is located in my own city, and when I mention that I hope no one will think it was put there because I happen to be in charge of this department; I mention it by way of illustration. By arrangement with the province that was thought to be one of the centres where such a clinic should be established. There is one in Cape Breton, ns another example. Last year, to use the figures for the clinic in my own city, over 1,000 children went through it. The psychiatrists, psychologists and social psychiatrists are paid out of funds provided by the national health program. The consequences to this nation of that kind of treatment I am sure will be of the greatest significance in the future.
The hon. member for Lanark quite properly pointed out the importance of research in this field. I can tell him that I am not satisfied with the progress we have made. Largely because of deficiencies in trained personnel, and not through any lack of desire to do
Supply-Health and Welfare something, the provinces have not been able to use as much of the mental health grant as is available to them now, and I hope steps can be taken by the provinces to make full use of it. 1 know we have helped provide over 3,000 trained persons under this program, a good number of whom will find their way into the provincial mental health divisions so they will be able to take up this work. Research is very important, of course, and I give as an example the Work being done by Dr. Ewen Cameron in Montreal. There we have given about $340,000 for research alone. We also assist the university of Montreal in its research in the field of psychiatry; we assist the university of Toronto. As my hon. friend said, this is a field in which the nation's resources may be well spent. He can be sure that if there is one field in which we are trying to provide direction and vigour, this is it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
281. Health insurance studies and administration of general health grants, $72,409.

Since the flurry we had about health insurance I have had an opportunity to read the evening newspaper, and the question of a health insurance scheme has been taken up by the Canadian Medical Association. I have not full information, but I believe they will make an honest attempt to do a good job. In the evening newspaper 1 notice two or three things that association is attempting to do, some of which strike me as very important. I do not know whether the minister will agree with the first one I am going to mention. This is an interview with Dr. McNulty, who said the government would be asked to pay the full cost of premiums of some sections of the population. The second point made is the free choice of doctors; and I was particularly taken with this statement:
It will protect the public and at the same time keep Canada's medical standards high.
Another point with which I was particularly pleased was the fact that they are working for reciprocity as between the provinces. I am sure this scheme will have a great deal to commend it, and that out of it we may be able to develop a great plan to cover the whole country. There may have to be additions, subtractions and changes, but I think we will all look forward to this plan in view of the fact that it is put forward by the doctors themselves, who I feel should be capable of dealing with this situation. For myself I will await full details with a great deal of interest.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

Supply-Health and Welfare AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Earlier today, Mr. Chairman, I had the privilege of paying a compliment to the hon. member for Lanark. It was a compliment that I was only too happy to pay, but I must now say that I cannot agree with the comments he made just before six o'clock. The hon. member made reference to reports in the press of today to the effect that the Canadian Medical Association is apparently going ahead with a private plan for prepaid medical care. If I understood the hon. member for Lanark correctly, he indicated that he had not seen all of the details of this plan and therefore did not wish to make a final commitment, but that in general he thought it might be a good idea.
Yesterday I had occasion to express my views with respect to this proposal. I did so because of a question and answer on the orders of the day yesterday morning. I made it clear last night that I felt that the whole question of health insurance should come under the aegis and under the administration of the governments of this country, recognizing that in the last analysis it will involve co-operation between the federal government and the governments of the various provinces. I feel, however, that it is extremely important that we get a statement from the Minister of National Health and Welfare with respect to this matter. He might say to me that another statement from him is unnecessary because of commitments he has made in the past to the principle of a program of health insurance for the people of Canada. But in view of this development at the meeting of the Canadian Medical Association I think it is timely that the Minister of National Health and Welfare have something to say on. this matter tonight.
One of the comments in the press with regard to this proposed plan is to the effect that the doctors would handle it under their own autonomous powers and that those who could afford to do so would pay their own premiums, but that the federal government would be asked to make contributions to the fund on behalf of those who could not afford to pay their own premiums. It seems to me that that is a case of this fine group of men, to whom I also paid a tribute this afternoon, getting out of their own field.
I have the highest respect for the work that doctors do in the field of medicine. I have personal reason to say that. I do not detract from it in any way. I am also extremely conscious of the great amount of work that doctors do for patients for which they get no

pay. I do not want to speak in language that would seem to make comparisons, but I am particularly aware of the way in which the doctors in my own city of Winnipeg carry on with respect to that phase of the matter. But when it comes to health insurance, when it comes to a plan to make possible the pooling of the costs of medical care, I am just as convinced as I believe is the Liberal party- judging from its official platform-and as I believe is the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that this is a matter that should come under the administration of the governments of this country.
For a number of years on the minister's estimates I have had occasion to prod him with regard to this item for health insurance studies. I am glad to note that the amount asked for has been increased a bit year by year, and that this year the amount asked for is greater than ever. I feel that it is particularly timely-indeed it is now urgent-that some action should be taken in the field of health insurance. From the newspaper reports it looks as though the aim of this plan proposed by the doctors is to head off what is referred to in the Ottawa Journal as socialized medicine. Even if there are some things about the doctors' plan that are good, it surely must be recognized by anyone who looks at it closely that it could be the enemy of something a great deal better.
We are spending money to provide for health insurance studies. The Liberal party is committed to the principle of health insurance. I need not go into the details about that again, for last night I read from what Mr. King had to say about that question at the Liberal convention of 1919. I also read from plank No. 11 which was adopted at the Liberal convention of 1948. I also read a statement made by the present Prime Minister in a national broadcast in December, 1948. The official position of the Liberal party is clear. I believe the position of the Minister of National Health and Welfare is clear. But what is lacking is action. We keep on asking questions and getting answers that mean nothing. We go on voting money for health insurance studies. But as yet we have not any real program of health insurance.
I should be happy if the minister would comment in general on the question of a health insurance program; and if he cares to do so, I should be glad if he would express any views he has with respect to the plan which has been reported recently in the press.

Mr. Chairman, I was absent
when the discussion took place earlier in the day. I happened to be at a committee meeting. I was not present when the

original flutter took place. May I say at once, in order to make it clear, that I am unalterably opposed to socialized or state medicine where the medical services, the workers and the doctors are state-controlled. I do not wish to see the relationship between the doctor and the patient destroyed. But I am in favour of a government-sponsored health insurance plan. We as a party are committed to an all-embracing social security program which included a health insurance plan, with special emphasis on medical, dental, surgical and hospital services. The Canadian people have for a long time demanded it and are expecting it. They are not as impatient as some people would indicate, but nevertheless they are expecting us to produce such a plan within a reasonable time.
The Canadian Medical Association have some plan of their own, and one of their spokesmen today said that prepayment medical schemes of the Canadian Medical Association will provide Canadians-and these are the words to which I direct attention-"with a better alternative to government health insurance." So far as I am concerned there is no alternative to government health insurance. Whatever they can do, we as a government can do better, cheaper, more satisfactorily, more uniformly and more in the public interest.

Is that the experience of
Great Britain?

I think you will find that that
is the experience in Great Britain. They are very well satisfied with it. As a matter of fact all the political parties in Great Britain support the health plans there. There is no political difference of opinion in Britain on the health plan, and there certainly is not any difference of opinion amongst the people. Originally there were some difficulties, which we are trying to profit by in Canada, by such actions as are taken by this government and the present minister in building up hospitals, facilities for training nurses and medical research of various kinds. At the appropriate time we will be able to go into a scheme on a fairly prepared basis.
I have no objection to the present voluntary medical schemes. I think they are good. In time I think they will provide us with valuable information for the development of our own national health scheme.
There can be no denial that the medical services today are woefully inadequate in this country, and the price for medical care in the market place is too high. We in this House of Commons must in some way find an answer to this problem. I do believe that
Supply-Health and Welfare medical care must come as a right and not as a dole. When we speak of over-all coverage we, the government of Canada, have more experience with respect to that than has anyone else. We have considerable experience in administering family allowances; we have considerable experience in administering old age pensions and unemployment insurance. There is not a body in all of Canada that has more experience in administering over-all coverage than have we in this House of Commons. In my short experience in this house I have come firmly to believe that our top civil servants in the government have as much administrative brains as has any other group in Canada.
I think our duty is to study and to explore and to find a solution to the financial riddle that lies at the heart of Canadian health.
I picked up some figures today having to do with the health of this country. I find that from 15,000 to 20,000 die yearly of ailments which could be cured or prevented by timely medical care; that a third of the people of Canada do not have the services of a family doctor, and wait too long before seeking medical care; and that only 20 per cent of the people of Canada are able to afford all the medical care that they need.
I think the Canadian Medical Association could well devote itself to building up the voluntary services across Canada; there is a great field there. But when they say-and I quote from the press-"We expect to give better service to the public than any government-sponsored scheme," then they are making a direct attack upon the plans that we have in mind and have had in mind for some time. They are confusing and misleading the public.
We are committed to a national health insurance plan. There can be no retreat from that. It is eminently clear to me that a national health plan is the very best medicine that money can buy. I do not want to hold up the committee, but I want to say this to the minister. The government, and he particularly, have been laying a very solid foundation for health insurance in this country. Their grants to hospitals, their inducement to building hospitals, their grants to health studies show that they have consistently attempted to create a situation that will make it possible for us to bring into being some day in the foreseeable future a national health plan which the people of this country are asking for, something that is in keeping with our all-embracing social security program. We had an example of it here today when hon. members from all sides of the house attempted to get on their feet as quickly as possible in order to give praise
4458	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare to a measure which was introduced by way of a resolution dealing with old age pensions.
I assure the minister that the health insurance program which the people of Canada have in their minds is equally important as the old age security program, and is expected by the people of Canada in a similar way. We should1 not disappoint them. I re-emphasize that the Canadian Medical Association is doing fine work, and should continue carrying on its voluntary work; but in so far as a national health plan is concerned, that is our job of work. They ought not to anticipate that they will ever take that over. If there is going to be any taking over, it will be done by us and not by them.

I find myself in agreement with some of the things that the hon. member for Spadina has said, but there is also a considerable part of his speech with which I cannot find agreement.
I think this action was taken by the doctors because they realized that something should be done about it. Personally, I have been advocating health insurance here for years, and as I mentioned this afternoon I saw the necessity for it. But I think the thing that was disturbing the Canadian Medical Association was their fear that under some scheme brought in the patient-doctor relationship would be disturbed. That is one thing on which they feel very strongly.
So far as the remarks of the hon. member are concerned, I wonder just what he meant when he said that the cost of medical care was too high. Surely, as a barrister, he did not intend to reflect on the fees charged by the medical people. I think what he meant to say was that the cost of hospital care and the cost of sickness have now gone beyond the reach of a great many people in Canada.
I do not think that any care for the sick can be a success in Canada unless you have the full co-operation of the Canadian Medical Association. It has taken them a long time to come to agreement on this matter, to come to agreement on certain things such as the matter of reciprocity between provinces. And when they brought forward this scheme it probably was in revolt against state medicine as administered in Great Britain.
A great deal of good may be-accomplished by any form of plan; and, as I said this afternoon, I am not going to pass judgment on this plan until I have seen the whole plan and have had time to pass on it. But I assure you, sir, that a body of men like the Canadian Medical Association are conversant with conditions in Canada. It is not so easy to come forward with a plan which would be a success in Canada. Our population is widely


distributed, and there would be problems arising from the geographical distribution of that population.
A great deal is being done free of charge at this time by the medical people in the outdoor departments of the hospitals, and I am still proud to say that the medical men have never hesitated to attend patients, whether they were able to pay fees or not. But when I find the Canadian Medical Association producing a plan, I am convinced it has not been done without having been first given a great deal of deliberation. I know they have discussed this matter for some years. They realize something should be done. They know the costs connected with running their hospitals, and they are familiar with the fact that almost all hospitals are running in the red. They realize, too, that there is need for treatment of a great many people in Canada who have not the opportunity for treatment. Therefore I suggest that before criticizing this plan it should be thoroughly investigated-because I am convinced no group of doctors representing the whole of Canada would bring in a plan made for the purpose of forwarding their own interests. I am sure the hon. member for Spadina will change his view when he sees some of the suggestions brought into the plan. Personally I have so much faith in the members of my own profession and in the deliberations that have taken place that I am content to wait. I think this will be a worthwhile plan, and will be of advantage to the citizens of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the minister comment on this matter?	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
This matter is one of some importance, and I had intended to say a word or two about it. With regard to the particular scheme that has given the discussion current interest, I think it is important not to attribute to it something that the doctors themselves have not attributed. Naturally over the course of many months I have had the opportunity of discussing this and many kindred problems with the medical profession.
Let me say at the outset that since I have been Minister of National Health and Welfare I have been inspired by the public spirit of the Canadian medical profession, and have recognized it as a profession that has rendered great service to humanity, and wishes to continue to do so. I feel that anything I say tonight should be prefaced with the observation that, no matter what scheme is envisaged to meet this social problem, it cannot succeed unless there is a great measure of collaboration between the medical

profession on one hand and governments and voluntary agencies on the other. It is in that spirit that I have approached my task, and it is in the same spirit that I have been received by the medical profession. As I have so frequently said in public, in any studies this government makes of this problem it will never embark upon a scheme that will disturb the very important doctor-patient relationship which I think good experience will indicate is very essential in any free society.
That has not been the case in other places; and where it has not been the case the result has been that schemes have been prejudiced and retrenchments have had to be resorted to, with the result that patterns created many years ago have been curtailed or destroyed as a result of extreme action. I think the thing to do in this problem is to realize that what is important is that a job be done; we can all argue in a free society that a job can be done better by one group or another, but the important thing is not who does the job, but that the job be done.
I have looked at this problem, and looked at it intensely for four and a half years, and it seems to me that those are the cardinal principles. I do not believe that anything that has emanated from the Canadian Medical Association, or from those who would take what might appear to be formally opposite views, is in disagreement on those points.
First, as to the scheme about which questions were asked yesterday of the Prime Minister, and about which so much has been said today, it is important to realize what has been discussed by the Canadian Medical Association. That was a scheme to induce various prepaid medical and hospital care plans across Canada to get together in order that they could sell a single insurance package to national agencies such as the banks, the railways and so on. There are in various provinces different programs involving different standards of fees, different coverage and differences in the number of agencies having to do with prepaid medical care. Obviously in these schemes that arise out of provincial charters based upon the supremacy of provincial parliaments in the field of property and civil rights, there is a lack of interchangeability between the operations of these prepaid medical plans as between one province and another, or between all provinces. And it is not unnatural tfiat to the extent that these programs go, there should be a desire to provide for national coverage.
Rather than indulge at this stage in a criticism of the proposed scheme, as though
Supply-Health and Welfare it were an effort to supplant particular objectives that have been declared to be the political objectives of various groups, one should look upon it, as I believe and know it to be, as a real and sincere attempt on the part of the medical profession to meet a problem which they recognize, just as we do.
These prepaid medical schemes have an admittedly limited coverage. They do not cover all phases of the problem,. In most of these particular prepaid medical schemes hospitalization is not included. Blue Cross does cover hospitalization; and I presume that if this proposed plan were ever to be realized there would have to be an integration of a program of that sort with these other prepaid medical plans.
Our studies-and they are important- indicate that a great burden lies in the matter of hospitalization. It may be for that reason that some provinces have embarked upon hospitalization schemes prior to adopting plans having to do with medical care insurance.
I believe one will do a disservice to the realization of this program unless one considers it carefully, step by step, irritating as that course may appear to be to some. But you can easily embark on a program, as in certain jurisdictions in this country it is now realized-, which creates great difficulty'

sufficient almost to jeopardize schemes well intentioned in their conception but seemingly very difficult in their operation.
As long as I have anything to do with this I propose to look at the question objectively without in any way setting aside the opinions which I personally may hold in respect to this matter. What we want to see, all of us regardless of political differences, is an arrangement in the country by which we can minimize the costs of the incidence of disease and, as sometimes happens, its crushing economic burden on the individual family or person.
It was with that in mind that we embarked in 1948 upon the national health program which I am bold enough to say, as a result of the co-operation we have had from the ten provincial governments, is effecting improvements in the health standards of the Canadian people which are away beyond the fondest hopes we had when that plan was created and announced by the Prime Minister of Canada at that time. I hope he will not mind my saying it, but as he is so close to me I will run the risk of incurring his criticism for saying that in my judgment this plan would never have been possible

Supply-Health and Welfare but for the very sincere and intense support given it by the present Prime Minister of Canada.
This program sought to provide, out of the consolidated fund of the country, moneys to assist the provinces in their already excellent health services, sometimes deficient for one reason or another and in most instances because of the lack of the necessary economic power. But we did embark on this program and sometimes we lose sight of its significance and extent.
In 1945 the federal government did make certain proposals to the provinces and among those proposals, apart from the general offer to assist in the matter of a national health insurance scheme initiated by the provinces, was the proposal for certain grants in aid in respect of the improvement of the general public health, the control of tuberculosis, cancer, crippling conditions in children, medical scientific research and hospital construction.
The extent of the offer in that particular in 1945 represented a total of $17,500,000. The plan that was announced in May of 1948 represented a total expenditure which was nearly twice the amount of the proposal made in 1945. The significance of that has often been overlooked in the discussion of this important matter. To the original scheme were added two operations that were not contemplated and not put forward to the provinces in 1945.
The first was assistance in the matter of cancer control. That was added. In the 1945 proposals, assistance was offered to the provinces in connection with hospital construction by way of loans at low interest rates to enable them to engage in a program of hospital construction. In the program announced in 1948 we made an offer to the provinces of a matching grant in cancer control and hospital construction because we were anxious to see construction take place. Instead of offering low interest loans we proposed to the provinces that we would make outright grants on the condition that they put up at least a like amount to assist in the building of hospital beds.
In the words of the American Public Health Association, which I know by heart because they have been an inspiration to us in the department in carrying on this work, this program represents "the most comprehensive step in the field of public health ever introduced by any federal state in the world." Those are most significant observations made by a neutral organization.
The result has been that in three and a quarter years, faced as we were with a shortage of hospital beds, 40,000 in number, in little over half of the five year objective
tMr. Martin.!

posed for ourselves, we have along with the provinces collaborated in the building of 30,000 additional hospital beds. You cannot have a health insurance scheme function successfully under any auspices unless you meet this problem of bed shortage. We have gone to the extent I have indicated toward meeting that most important and necessary prerequisite. When the Prime Minister announced this program in 1948 he referred to the whole program as a prerequisite of a system of health insurance in Canada.
Not only have we helped build these hospital beds, we have supplied the ten provincial governments health personnel to the extent of over 3,000. I wonder if hon. members appreciate the significance of that. Three thousand additional persons have been employed in the health field, in public health units and in the various provincial departments of health, as a result of financial assistance given under this program.
I am sure that hon. members realize the significance of the training program that is under way. We are short of nurses in Canada to the extent of 8,000, and we are also short, as are other countries, of other personnel in the health field to the extent of many hundreds and, in some instances, many thousands. Under this program we have given assistance to over 900 nurses who presumably would have found it difficult to obtain training but for the program.
We have now actually given bursary assistance to not less than 2,800 individuals. This bursary assistance is being given in our medical centres, in our public health centres, and in occupational therapy centres at the universities. But for this assistance many of these persons might not have been able to continue with their training.
We have supplied our hospitals with equipment of all kinds running into millions of dollars which otherwise might not have been purchased. I am sure hon. members from Prince Edward Island who know something of the problem there with regard to mental illness will be able to corroborate what I am saying in that regard. In this rich province of Ontario, to use the words of the premier of the province, were it not for the assistance given under this plan they would not have been able to embark upon the accelerated program of public health activities that has gone on in Ontario during the past two years.
We should think of the work that was being done in the field of medical scientific research before this program came into being when only $350,000 was being expended on medical research. Today under this program that figure is close to $3 million. When this program began, in the field of cancer

research there were but two programs of significance. Today there are ninety-two under way in our various medical centres at our Canadian universities. All those are facts of the greatest significance gradually leading up to the time when we can competently deal with this program, not irresponsibly, not because we want to satisfy political fancy or some theoretical concept of the role of the state, but because we will be in a practical position to deal with this important problem. I believe that unless it is approached in that way we would do more harm than good.
But there is this further consideration. We are a federal state. We have ten provincial governments which have been endowed with the constitutional responsibility of directing health policy in their jurisdictions. Anyone who has had anything to do with dominion-provincial relations-and I may say that I have had my share in the past four and a half years-knows full well that any scheme we adopt must be one that will be followed by the co-operation of the provinces of Canada. I have talked to the representatives of every one of the ten provinces of Canada about this matter. I know this, of the ten provinces, that until such time as we are ready and equipped we Will not get their co-operation. Indeed some provinces, for reasons best known to themselves, take the view that this is not the way to deal with this problem.
No man who holds my responsibility would be able to bring in any scheme successfully by using the iron heel with respect to the provinces because in some instances they have a deep and special philosophy of life. I believe that one cannot do things in a federal state except by co-operation. My views in this matter are well known. They have not lost one iota of their zeal, and it is because of that that I propose, as long as I am in this position, to discharge this responsibility with those considerations in mind, knowing that as a result we are more likely going to be able to share in the success than in the failure of the realization of our objective.
We have under way now two important surveys that have not been mentioned today. One of the offers made by the national health program was that we agreed to assume the full cost of a survey in each province in the whole field of public health. These surveys are under way in every one of our provinces. I had hoped that they would be concluded before now but they are not. Three provinces have made interim reports, and they have asked us not to disclose their contents yet. In two instances recommendations are made in the reports of the surveys to the provincial
Supply-Health and Welfare governments, and the provincial governments naturally want to consider the implications of the recommendations before we can make them public. The other seven reports, which have to do with the whole business of the pursuit of health-and that is a complicated business-will be ready, I hope, some time this fall for scrutiny, and for consideration by the provincial governments.
There is another survey that in one sense is of even greater significance. I announced during the last session of parliament that we had undertaken a sickness survey in Canada.
I am told that no other country in the world has undertaken such a program. That survey is now under way, and has been under way for about six and a half months. Some of its interim conclusions are before me, but I believe until they have been finally and fully reported it would be unfair to make their content known. That survey, conducted by the federal government through the co-operation of the provinces and at our expense, is intended to reveal a statistical showing of morbidity and health in this country of a very extensive character. It will show the cost of health care. No province today can adequately show that, and all provinces readily concur in the objective of the sickness survey.
It will reveal not only the incidence of disease, the extent, for instance, of incapacity, and the income earning position of individuals with respect to matters of medical and hospital care as well as the income capacity of individuals who are disabled. The purpose is so that we will know in that particular, as in all others, what the problems are that we must face. These are steps that are being taken by the government, steps that are consistent with the position that we have taken at all times with regard to this matter, and we will continue through these agencies, through our own health insurance studies, the staff for which has been augmented and the budget for which has been increased, the program of giving proper assessment to this problem. The objective of all these efforts is to arrive at the most responsible measure of determining the best way of minimizing the cost of medical and hospital care in Canada.
Our position in this matter is well known. The background that I have given is necessary to a knowledge of this problem. It does not in any way involve a change in attitude, but it does involve a determination to know what all the facts are. I do not believe that we would make any progress in this matter if we were to overestimate public acceptance of this problem or of its relation to national financial capacity. Some hon. members may take the view that we

Supply-Health and Welfare should do all these things at once. I am firmly of the opinion that these things cannot all be done at once. We have embarked upon a big program today, a program of the greatest significance, and I believe that the experience of practically every country in the world will reveal that these problems are solved not by bold declarations of intention but by careful step-by-step action. That, I believe, is what the Canadian people believe in, and I believe that they will have confidence in that approach rather than one that seeks to build up a situation suddenly overnight that could result in providing a lack of proper balance with respect to what I think our Canadian pattern requires, a balance between security and freedom.
Therefore we will examine the proposal of the Canadian Medical Association just as it was examined in 1943 when they came before the Heagerty committee and gave us their views in which they expressed their general agreement with the principle of health insurance. We will examine that problem, and in the regular session of 1952 I hope that we may be able-and I think I may go further than that and say that we are giving consideration to the matter-to set up a parliamentary committee to examine this whole problem.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that
what I have said tonight should indicate, first of all, the government's sincere intention with respect to the problem that is involved here. We want to approach it in a way that will not cause the discordant notes that have been caused elsewhere. I know something about those notes. I have talked to some of the men who had the responsibility for the administration of schemes in some of these countries. We want to profit from some of their experience, as I am sure we all do. What we want to do is develop in the Canadian way, slowly perhaps but I think generally soundly, a responsible attitude and pattern that will not cause any real break between one section of the Canadian community and another. I believe that to be important.
As I review this problem in perspective I realize the difficulty there was in obtaining free education in a free society, and the same sort of problem exists with regard to this matter of equalizing the cost of medical and hospital care. We can do that and we will do that, undoubtedly co-operatively with the provincial governments and the health profession, in a manner that will be true to our


political objectives, to our political declarations, and always, as I believe they should be, in the true Canadian tradition.

The minister has been dealing with a very important question, in a way one of the most important questions facing the people of Canada today. He said that he was looking at the matter objectively, but I had a feeling that his words had an undertone indicating that the rest of us who were advocating something different were looking at things from preconceived political concepts; I think these were the words he used. If the minister expects us to accept his sincerity in this matter, the first requisite is that he should accept ours. What we are advocating we believe to be not only in the line of progress but to be imperative in that progress. I listened to him very intently and I am satisfied that if he has proven any one point it is this, that today the people of Canada as individuals, by and large, cannot pay for the medical and hospital services they require out of their own resources.
Step by step the government of Canada and the provinces have been obliged to come in to assist the people to get that medical care and the hospital services that today we consider not only desirable but absolutely necessary. He said that his policy, the government's policy, was to proceed step by step. I have no objection to this step by step approach. As a matter of fact, I am in favour of the step by step approach. But if you are going anywhere by the step by step method, the question of how soon you get there depends upon how quickly those steps follow each other. The trouble with the minister's step by step approach is that he is thinking of the step by step age that has passed, the age of the oxcart and not the step by step age of the aeroplane, the rocket and the wireless. If the minister knows anything of historic development, he knows that man's progress has moved at the same rate as his means of transportation.
When man had no other means of taking himself from one place to another except by walking, it took thousands of years for certain things to happen. Then came the use of the horse, and progress was made a little faster. Then came the railroad engine, and things moved faster still. Then came the gasoline engine, and the aeroplane and so on, and things are moving so fast today none of us knows exactly where he is.
I suggest to the minister that this country is not likely to get a policy from the medical profession that will provide prepaid services for everyone who needs medical services without the state organizing that service.

What is happening today is that the cost of medical and health services has increased to a point where it is beyond the resources of the majority of individuals, and this is true to a greater extent than it was twenty or twenty-five years ago. Anyone who has given any thought to this matter knows that we are not likely to get the assistance of the medical profession in any program we set up to provide medical and hospital services for everyone. It took years to get that any place where it has been accomplished, and perhaps no country has yet got it in a full measure because the medical profession has a -vested interest in things as they are. While that applies it is not natural to expect them to be interested in some other scheme of health service.
There is one thing, however, that has been settled, and that is wherever these schemes have been tried the people will never go back to the old way of doing things. In New Zealand, the United Kingdom, even with the opposition of the medical profession, progress has been made in supplying health services for everyone regardless of means. There would be no thought of any government that might follow the governments that are in office in those countries today throwing overboard what has been done, and going back to the old way of each person paying for his own medical services.	I suggest to the
minister that he keep these things in mind, and also keep in mind that those of us who are advocating something different are not doing so solely because of preconceived political concepts. We have made a study of these matters just as he has. Not only that, but we come in contract daily with people who cannot pay for the medical services they need. As we see these things we realize that there is only one way in which it can be done, and that is by the people doing collectively for themselves what they are not able to do for themselves as individuals. That is, in essence, what government means.

I have just one question I should like to ask the minister. He stated that no medical scheme could be a success in Canada, or in any other country for that matter, without the collaboration of the medical profession. I think we all agree with him in that statement. This parliament agreed with him in it in 1942 and 1943 when we had the Heagerty committee to which he has referred. That committee called before it the medical profession and heard from them. They heard evidence from hospital associations. In fact, they consulted everybody who they thought might be able to give them some good advice on this matter.
Supply-Health and Welfare The medical profession are now proposing a scheme in which they are going to ask the government to do certain things. As is stated here in the press report:
. . . the government would be asked to pay the full cost of premiums of some sections of the population, and part premiums on a sliding scale for others, based on income.
I wonder if the medical profession did as this parliament did, namely consult the minister's department on this matter before making this announcement? I do not know. I suppose the minister could not answer for the provinces, but he certainly could answer for the government and for his own department.

My hon. friend will know that the next step was-
We were prepared to consult with them. I am asking whether they were prepared to consult with us.

That was not my question at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If I have not answered it, I am sorry.
I understand that we are a federal state. What I asked was this: Was the minister's department consulted with respect to this scheme announced by the medical profession?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: In the precise terms, no. But I do not want that answer to be construed as meaning that the medical profession were not anxious to consult with us or that they have not collaborated and consulted with us. They have.

Mr. Chairman, it was a great, consolation to those of us who sit here, hale and hearty, to have the minister's assurance that we are living in just about the best of all possible worlds, and that we have about the best possible medical, health and hospitalization scheme administered by the best possible Minister of National Health and Welfare. It is a great consolation to us to know that. But the tens of thousands of people in Canada who have been paying into some of these prepaid insurance schemes, some of whom have been waiting for months to get a hospital bed, will not find so much consolation in the minister's speech. The minister, with his usual dexterity, skated completely around the one question to which we wanted an answer. That question is whether the government as such has abandoned Liberal policy going back thirty years with regard to national health insurance. Has the government abandoned the policy of establishing national health insurance under government administration, and has it agreed to accept instead the scheme which has now been announced by the Canadian Medical Association? The Prime Minister's reply to questions yesterday would indicate that that is exactly what has happened to this Liberal government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is the hon. member's interpretation.
That is my interpretation,.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: But that is not true.

That is my interpretation and it is the interpretation of a great many other people in this country. There was nothing whatever in the minister's speech tonight to indicate that that is not the position of the government. The minister did not come out with a clear-cut statement to say that he and his department were still backing a national health insurance scheme instituted and administered by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Apparently the hon. member did not hear what I said.

I certainly did not hear- and I doubt if anyone else did either-the minister come out with a straightforward statement in that respect. That is one question that we wanted answered.
I am not surprised that the Canadian Medical Association have come forward with the scheme which they have announced. I suspect that many thousands of Canadian doctors are just sick and tired of waiting for this government really to do something in the matter of health insurance. They are sick and tired of seeing thousands of their patients unable to get into hospital beds and unable to pay doctors' and hospital bills. This government has been dilly-dallying with this question of health insurance, and has been going, as the minister says, step by step for over thirty years. But those steps have not taken them much closer to the realization of a genuinely national health insurance scheme than we have ever been. I am not critical of the Canadian Medical Association. I hope that the effect of their announcement will be to spur this government into some little action in this matter. I hope that the effect of this announcement will be to induce the minister and his colleagues really to get down to earth in the planning of a national health insurance scheme.
The minister tells us that we cannot have such a national health insurance scheme until we get enough hospital beds to accommodate the people. Some of these groups operating these prepaid schemes have been taking the money of Canadians for years and promising hospitalization; yet even today many of those who have been paying for that insurance find themselves unable to get into a hospital. Only today I was speaking to a patient here in the house. He had been paying into one of these schemes, and had to wait for a month to get into a hospital. The doctors are not saying that we have to wait until we have beds enough to accommodate all the Canadian sick before instituting some such scheme. They propose to have one-half of their scheme operating within a year and to have the full scheme covering both medical care and hospitalization in effect in less than two years. If they can do that, and apparently the minister and certainly the Prime Minister hope that they can, and the Prime Minister has given them his blessing to proceed, then why must the government wait for another thirty years before they undertake to institute a national health insurance scheme?
I have no doubt that, whatever type of scheme is eventually adopted, it will be a better one not because of the research that the minister's department has put into it,

but because of the study that the Canadian Medical Association has given the subject over the past seven years. While the government has been giving the Canadian people, in their propaganda, information leading them to believe that we were going to have a government health insurance scheme, the Canadian Medical Association has been quietly studying and discovering how that scheme can best be put into effect. I am confident that eventually some scheme will be adopted which will be better because of that study.
I would urge the minister to reconsider this whole question. From anything I know of the small section of the Canadian people with whom I come in contact, I can say that they do not want a health scheme organized and administered by the Canadian Medical Association.
The association proposes to institute a scheme whereby the government will pay for a part of the population. They propose to enrol the entire population of Canada in their scheme, with the government paying for all those in the lower income groups. One of their officers indicated that no person receiving less than $2,400 a year could possibly afford to pay medical and hospital bills, and suggested that the government might pay for those below that category. Are we to have a scheme organized and administered by the Canadian Medical Association, and a large part of that scheme paid for out of the Canadian taxpayers' money through the federal and provincial governments? I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that is not the type of health insurance that the Canadian people want. That is not the type of health insurance that the Liberal party have been promising to Canadian people over the past thirty years.

This is as good an item as
any on which to congratulate the minister and his able officials on the considerable expansion that has taken place during the past six years in the departmental activities of the Department of National Health and Welfare, and also on the considerable benefits which have accrued thereby to the less fortunate in this land.
Under the able guidance of the minister, Canada is heading towards a comprehensive plan of social security. It may be going, as some hon. member have said, step by step, but most of us recognize that in most things in life that is the safest way to proceed. The accomplishments of this government, and of the minister in particular, in the last number of years have proven that the advance has been steady, even if it was step by step.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Great improvements have accrued to the provinces through the provincial grants and to the people of Canada in general through the medical facilities extended throughout the country, which have come from the help given the provinces to strengthen their position. One has only to read the report of the departmental activities in the Department of National Health and Welfare to realize what has been done in the past few years. When it comes to the national health program I think the steps that have been taken, as well as those that are contemplated, are proper and in the right direction.
In this house I represent a rural constituency. Each time I visit the different villages that make up the constituency I can visualize the need for a health insurance program. I visualize the difficulty these people experience in having their sick people treated. It is not for me to criticize the hospital costs and the charges made in the different parts of the country or in different parts of my province, but whatever may be the cause these costs are unbearable by quite a number of people. When they come to you asking for help in trying to present their case to the hospital authorities you can realize the burden in general for all of those people and even those who do not dare to approach you, and you can realize that within a limited number of years the people of Canada will expect that a program of health insurance will be put forward by this government not on a Canadian Medical Association professional basis but on a governmental basis, as it should be, with the co-operation that the medical profession in general has shown, as the minister says, and with good will towards its realization, even if resolutions have been passed lately that have called for some comments by hon. members.
I think this may also be an opportune time, since we are studying health insurance, to tell the minister that some of us may be slightly disappointed that no proposals have yet been brought to the house concerning a definite approach to pensions for the infirm or the invalids. Some hon. gentlemen, probably more conversant with the question than I am, have said in the past that invalidity or infirmity pensions should come forward at the same time as health insurance. While this has not been so in many countries that have already adopted invalidity pensions, yet I think the time has come, whether the government is ready or not, or the studies are ripe or not, to bring in a scheme of health insurance, to consider seriously at one of the very early sessions bringing before us a program of invalidity pensions. I think I am quite in order in bringing this up at this
