Supply-Health and Welfare time, because it has been said so often that this should be analysed seriously with the help of the medical profession and in connection with a health insurance program.
I think that the house is unanimous in its resolve to support the government in any scheme for invalidity pensions. I have already spoken on the matter on three different occasions in the house: in 1946, in 1949 and in 1950. In those years, along with my colleagues, I advocated the necessity of invalidity pensions. I think we are all agreed on the need of doing something as early as we can. Last year, when I congratulated the minister on the appointment of a committee to deal with old age security, I said that I was much disappointed that the minister had not seen fit to put this question, together with the question of old age security or amendments to the Old Age Pensions Act, before us. At the time they were talking about a dominion-provincial conference; yet, if my information is correct, the program for the conference had not been definitely settled. At this session the minister answered the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to the effect that we could not deal with the matter at this session because the subject of invalidity pensions was not on the program of the dominion-provincial conference.
But, Mr. Chairman, I think the time has come when this matter should be examined seriously by the minister and the government. I understand that not very long ago a conference was held in Toronto with respect to the rehabilitation of invalids and infirm people. That may be the first step in the right direction; it might lead to some hope for agreement that may bring about the scheme we all want to see introduced in Canada. But I think we will need: to stress upon the minister the urgency of acting quickly and of tackling the problem as early as we can.
I have heard two arguments voiced against an invalidity pensions scheme, namely the difficulty of applying it and, secondly, the cost. As to the question of difficulty we were told it would be better to wait until the health insurance plan was brought forward, because the same physicians and departmental administrative staffs could be used, and that the work of both could be done at the same time. But it may be, as one hon. member has said, that it will take a little time before we have definitely a health insurance program; the step might take a little longer than some of us wish. Therefore I wonder if the minister would not consider studying seriously in the immediate future 

the possibility of doing for the infirm and invalids what some other countries have done in this regard.
It is said that there would be difficulty in applying such a law. Last year, although the question of invalidity was not included in the agenda of the joint committee on old age security, I was allowed to ask a few questions and to ask for the production of information with respect to invalidity schemes that had been carried out in other countries. I find that invalidity schemes have been working satisfactorily and are working at the moment in Australia, Denmark, New Zealand and Sweden. If such countries have been able to tackle the problem, I do not see why we cannot do it right away.
If I may be given a few moments-and I shall make my remarks as brief as possible- I would say that in Australia the first legislation in this regard, concerning invalidity, was passed in 1910, and that is quite a few years ago. I shall not place all the material I have on record, but for the information of hon. members the details are to be found in the minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 29, of the committee on old age security, 1950.
In respect to Australia the qualifying conditions are as follows: age 16, and permanently incapacitated for work; at least 85 per cent disability, or permanently blind.
In Canada we already have a pension for the blind. Why could we not administer an invalidity or infirmity scheme as well as our scheme for pensions for the blind? Doctors could be trusted just as much to declare a man or woman invalid as they can be trusted to declare blindness.
Then, to carry on with the qualifying conditions in Australia: incapacity must have occurred in that country, and it is waived if there is twenty years of residence. There must be continuous residence in the country for at least five years, and the person must be of good character.
In Denmark the act is dated 1933. In January 1946 there were 41,800 recipients. In a moment or so I shall give more details with respect to the number of recipients in Australia, because I have some further comments to make about it. In Denmark, the qualifying conditions are the following: These pensions are payable from ages 14 to 65 inclusive. Recipients must be unable to earn one-third of the amount earned by persons with similar training and skill in the same locality. The income limit is the same as for old age pensions. The applicant must be of good character.

In New Zealand the scheme was brought about in 1936. The qualifying conditions are: age, 16 to 60; permanent incapacity for work through accident, illness or congenital defect, or totally blind. Incapacity may not be self-inflicted. There must be a residence for ten years immediately preceding the date of application for benefits.
In Sweden the act dates back to 1913, and it is currently governed by the National Pensions Act of 1946. The same law as to privileges apply as in respect of old age pensions. The qualifying conditions are: age 16 to 66, inclusive; permanently incapable of self-support in work corresponding to experience and training. Housing and housewife's benefits are subject to income tests, the same as old age pensioners. There is a blindness supplement, paid without income test to persons who have become blind before reaching the age of 60. There is a sickness allowance, with a disablement the same as for invalidity, lasting at least one year but not deemed permanent. The communes pay part of the cost of pensions supplements.
If these countries have found it possible to administer such a scheme and if the medical profession has been able to help them carry it through, I do not see why in Canada we cannot do the same, when most of us realize in our own constituencies the great need for such a pension.
Then, as to cost, may I be permitted at this point to bring in a few details concerning the Australian scheme, so that we may determine what it might cost for a similar scheme in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am grateful for the information the hon. member is giving, but I would point out that we are dealing with the item of health insurance studies and that perhaps the hon. member should confine his remarks to that item. If I did not rise, I am sure some other hon. member would do so, and perhaps I would be subject to criticism.

Mr. Chairman, there are two
or three things I should like to say before this item carries. I have been intensely interested in all that has been said since the debate on this item commenced. My colleagues and I have on innumerable previous occasions indicated our belief that some form of health insurance is appropriate. However, I would hasten to add that that does not imply that we are prepared to accept any type of health insurance that someone may desire to impose upon us, nor are we asking that we plunge into a scheme of health insurance overnight. We have had a certain amount of experience in our own country which should have taught us something.
We are convinced that the necessary hospital construction is imperative. We realize that no scheme could succeed without an adequate number of hospital beds. We realize fully that no scheme can succeed without an adequate number of qualified doctors, nurses and other personnel to manage our hospitals.
I listened with intense interest to the minister's reference to the grants which had been made to the provinces under the legislation of 1948. I do not know whether it is just an unfortunate habit of the minister,

Supply-Health and Welfare but after paying a tribute to what the provinces were doing he repeatedly created the impression that most of what is being done is being done by the federal government. We have built these beds; we have built those beds. Some of the minister's colleagues have contracted that same-I should not say disease, although it may be appropriate since we are discussing health measures- what I might term a habit.
I recall only too well that last fall I participated in a provincial by-election in my own constituency. Some of those who think similarly to the minister along political lines were asserting on every platform, "Yes, you have more hospitals, but who built them? We did. We have put up all kinds of money. True you have more of this and more of that, but who paid for it? We did".
Let me assure the minister that long before these health grants were made available to my province we had made vast strides in the field of hospital construction and the advancement of other essential health services. I hasten to add that my province is certainly most grateful for the assistance which has been made available through the national health grant.
When one comes from a community such as mine and hears people state what they have to pay for hospital and medical services in other parts of Canada, right here in Ottawa for example, he is almost shocked. I come from a community in which dollar a day hospitalization is the order of the day. Only two and a half years ago, I happened to be hospitalized myself and had what you might characterize as a private room. It cost me $1 per day while I was there. When I find that people have to pay $8, $9 and $10 a day for a hospital room, I am shocked. Moreover, I have no difficulty in securing a hospital bed in my own town. Yet I learn that it is customary in this city and elsewhere, unless the case is an extremely serious one, to make a reservation at the hospital, the same as you would at a hotel in a busy city, two or three months in advance. When I hear that, I certainly am shocked.
I do not know how true this is, but some young friends of mine in this city told me that when their first child was born it cost them between $250 and $300. I was shocked to hear that, because in my home town hospitalization for that kind of case is absolutely free and the medical services would be approximately $55. In other words, practically the entire cost would be only $55. The thought that enters my mind is how in the world can a substantial proportion of the people meet these costs. They simply


cannot. Unless the municipality is prepared to assume the greater part of the burden I suppose their bedrooms become their hospital rooms.
I was interested in certain observations made by the hon. member for Spadina. He said that he is opposed to socialized state medicine. So am I. I am opposed to what I would define as socialized state medicine. I think it is most desirable, as the minister and others have asserted, that we should try to preserve the doctor-patient relationship. I do not want to see any scheme put into operation that will result in the rigid regimentation of doctor, patient or nurse. That is the position I have taken from the beginning.
If I were to indicate what I considered to be the ideal situation it would be to have such economic conditions as would permit the individual to choose his own doctor, his own hospital and pay his own bill. That would be the ideal situation. However, we realize that thousands of people are not in the position where that can be done and it therefore becomes' necessary to provide a certain degree and type of service for them. I want to see the preservation of that thing which induces doctors to give service wherever and whenever it may be required.
I certainly commend the government for the assistance it is giving through these health grants, but I think the provinces which meet these grants dollar for dollar should also be commended.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is for cancer control and hospital construction only.

I welcomed the minister's announcement that a committee would be set up during the session of 1952. We commend the minister for having indicated that that will be the government's course and we shall look forward to serving on the committee and making whatever contribution we can toward bringing into being in Canada a system which will provide a service and at the same time preserve the freedom of the Canadian people, including the doctors, nurses and hospital administrators.

Mr. Chairman, as one who has taken great interest in this subject throughout the years and who has seen the great need in his own constituency for some form of national health insurance, I must for once become vocal on this subject. I listened with great interest to the minister's step by step explanation and definition of government policy which I am quite sure left many of us quite uncertain as to what the government intends to do. My impression is that the step by step policy is one of marking time, his speech very different to the type of speech we heard in 1945 and prior to 1945. I am quite sure the minister realizes that public opinion in Canada is prepared for government action in the direction of national health insurance. All parties in this house are committed to the principle of national health insurance. During the last federal election all parties placed it in their programs and informed the electorate they would support the principle of health insurance when they returned to the House of Commons.
All organized labour in Canada has expressed support for the principle of national health insurance. For quite a number of years the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, representing the farmers organizations of Canada, has endorsed the principle of national health insurance and has done a great deal of work in this connection. If I remember correctly, I think the federation published a very interesting and informing booklet on the subject in 1944. The Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations from the Pacific to the Atlantic have endorsed the principle of national health insurance and throughout the years have urged the government to take action. In view of the mass of public support for action on this matter, in view of the wealthy nature of our economy, and realizing what has been done in European countries throughout the years in the matter of national health insurance, countries with far less wealth than we have, far less production per capita, surely we in Canada, intending to vote estimates totalling some $3,700 million this year, can with the co-operation of the provinces at least commence to take action with respect to national health insurance.

I should like to ask the
minister a question concerning a matter which I brought up some time ago, and that is the Campbellton-Cross Point bridge. I believe

Supply-Public Works the premier of New Brunswick was reported as stating that the responsibility for building this bridge rested entirely with the federal government. At the time the minister was not certain whether or not it was a federal responsibility. He intimated that he would obtain a decision from the Department of Justice.
In this connection, I should like to read what the premier of New Brunswick is reported to have said to the local legislature at Fredericton. He said:
The building of the bridge is not the responsibility of the New Brunswick government, nor the Quebec government.
I might say that this bridge is between Campbellton, New Brunswick and Cross Point, Quebec.
It is a federal matter. This was clearly evident in the provisions of the British North America Act, and it was reiterated in 1945 when the federal spokesmen informed the provinces: "The dominion government is now responsible for . . . interprovincial and international bridges." Premier Duplessis of Quebec supports this view.
Then the premier of New Brunswick went on to say:
The do-nothing policy of the federal government in the case of the Campbellton bridge follows a familiar pattern of apathy towards New Brunswick's just claims. Ottawa is simply "passing the buck,"
The minister rather questioned this statement when I made it before. I am quoting directly from the premier of New Brunswick. The item that he referred to is an item in "Public Investment", a blue book or green book issued by the federal government for the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction in 1945. At page 42 this statement will be found under the paragraph headed "Highways and Bridges":
Highways and bridges, when situated wholly within a province, come under provincial jurisdiction but where they connect two provinces or extend beyond the limits of the province, they become a federal responsibility, under section 92 (10) of the British North America Act.
The paragraph continues:
By the same act, military roads were placed under dominion control by authority of section 91 (7) . . .
But that is the section that the premier of New Brunswick refers to. I had a reply not from the Minister of Public Works but from the deputy minister of justice. This letter I received from him is dated May 26, 1951, and reads as follows:
Re: Construction of bridge between Campbellton, New Brunswick and Cross Point, Quebec.
Dear Sir:
There has been referred to me for attention, a request which I understand you have made to the Minister of Public Works for an opinion on a question in connection with the construction of a bridge
[Mr. Brooks.)
between Campbellton, New Brunswick and Cross Point, Quebec.
I have to advise that I am of the opinion that legislative jurisdiction over interprovincial works of this nature belongs to parliament,-
I interpret that as meaning the federal parliament.
-and executive authority to the federal cabinet.
From this rather vague letter of the deputy minister I think it is quite evident that his opinion is that interprovincial bridges are the responsibility of the federal government. I should like to ask the minister if he himself has looked into the matter. Probably he has not felt the necessity of doing so because, from what I read here in 1945, evidently a legal opinion was given at that time that the responsibility for interprovincial bridges was that of the federal government.
I should like to ask the minister if he has made, or if he intends to make, any provision for the construction of this necessary bridge between Campbellton and Cross Point. A ferry had been running there for quite a number of years. The people in that area found it inadequate as far as service to the people was concerned. The ferry was destroyed slightly over a year ago, and that area is now served by neither a bridge nor a ferry. I know that the people in that area have sent in petitions and that there is in the minister's office considerable correspondence in connection with the construction of this bridge. I should like to ask him if anything is being done at the present time.

In Burin-Burgeo the amount is $443,120; in Grand Falls-White Bay, $159,600; in Humber-St. George's-again small potatoes compared with the others, but very much higher than ours-$78,400, and in Trinity-Conception, $529,500. I am not going to labour the point, but I should like to make this comment. We came into union with Canada in 1949. Since then the grand total is over three and a half million. That is including the proposed current expenditure of $2,704,058. Of that amount the district of the Secretary of State alone receives these two amounts, $267,095.21 and $1,332,575. I am a person that believes that lightning does not usually strike twice in the same place. In 1949, in the month of December, the minister said, in answer to my leader, that it was a very peculiar coincidence that moneys for public works were

expended as they were in Newfoundland. I again ask him tonight to explain how that coincidence could have happened again.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not wish to make a lengthy statement, but I will try to come right down to the point. I am told that St. John's, Newfoundland, had its harbour facilities kept in good condition all through the last war. Reports received from the engineers would not have justified expenditures, even if we tried to divide public works estimates pro rata to the population; but we were told- and I have reports from the engineers to that effect-that the outlying coast where the fishermen make their living had no harbour facilities. I am told that they are the poor element of the population. From the kindness of heart of my officials we thought we would start doing work in Newfoundland to help these poor fishermen. When we get to St. John's where the facilities exist my hon. friend can rest assured that I will not forget my two good friends from St. John's. If they have any special requests that are justified according to the reports I receive from the engineers there would be no distinction because they do not belong to the government party. You can take my word for that because I have been following that policy for seven years.

Either the minister's milk of human kindness has been curdled or he has been badly misinformed because the constituencies of St. John's East and St. John's West are not only city districts but take in outlying fishing settlements as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is where we spent that money.

As the minister knows, or should know, requests have been made on behalf of the fishermen of these districts for various facilities, but they have not been acceded to. I will mention one in particular in my own riding, and that is Flat Rock, where there is a very large fishing settlement, from which a request was made, and I myself was informed that the cost of doing the job there would be $150,000. That was considered to be too high for the work to be done by the department. That is perfectly all right. So long as the minister says he is not going to do it in the city of St. John's, all right. The city will look out for itself. But what about the fishermen he is so interested in? He has told us how interested he is in helping the fishermen. I ask him, in that case, to take into consideration the settlement of Flat Rock, and also the settlement of Bauline.
Bauline has made a request for a breakwater, but that request has not yet been

acceded to. There is a very hard-working and liberal-minded group of people in Bauline; I can assure the minister of that. They certainly would be more than happy if he were to agree to their request.
Then he should be happy to consider the annual question of the wharf at Portugal Cove. The minister has been pretty generous in his treatment of certain districts, and in particular his treatment of that district represented by the Secretary of State. I do not blame him; after all, the Secretary of State is very close to him. Probably he has the minister's ear more than other Newfoundland members associated with him-and certainly more than the hon. member for St. John's West and myself.
He must remember, as I have tried to tell him more than once, that Bell Island is most important, and that Bell Island needs to be serviced by this wharf. I would remind him that Bell Island is still the largest iron ore mine in the British empire today. I would remind him that the war effort requires the use of all possible facilities. Merely because the minister states Portugal Cove wharf is a ferry wharf, the minister says he will not help put a proper wharf there. I have asked for the correspondence in this connection, and the minister has put me off by saying that it was not agreed to by the premier of Newfoundland. Then the other day he said that the premier had agreed.
I still have not got the correspondence, and I still do not know what happened, and I hope the minister will tell me what happened when he gets a chance. Maybe he will tell me tonight. He has told me that I have no fishermen in my constituency, and that there are none in the constituency of the hon. member for St. John's West. But other constituencies have been receiving large expenditures because of fishing settlements. Perhaps the minister would explain that.
Mr. Four mar (Hull):	Public works proceed gradually throughout the country. If the hon. member were to see the files in our office, containing requests from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Victoria on Vancouver island, he would be surprised how many works we do not cope with every year. But I like the way the hon. member deals with the estimates of this department, because it brings me back to reality. Only a few days ago I read a newspaper from his city, the Sunday Herald, which I believe circulates in all Newfoundland, and is the largest newspaper on the island.

Which island?
Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Newfoundland. Do
you know what they say about public works? They say this:
Although not too much is heard on the subject, it's a fact that hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent in this province on federal public works since confederation. But you would have to travel around the country to see the dozens of public wharves which have been constructed at Ottawa's expense. Today, even the most remote hamlet-
And this is speaking of Newfoundland-
-has a jetty which is only slightly too small for the Queen Mary. And we cannot help but wonder if a great many of these wharves are not a waste of money.
May I ask a question?

speechtext: No. Just a moment. I hope my hon. friend made requests to me tonight that will be justified. Do not mind what party you belong to: if the need is there, we are at your service.

The minister does drip like a honeydew melon, and one cannot be upset by him. He has such a kindly voice. However, I would like to ask if he quoted the newspaper as an authority. I ask him that because it is a paper that is very close to the party in power in Newfoundland, and some may question its authenticity.
Its objectivity.

Yes, its objectivity. Let me say that the engineer of the department, Mr. Gerald Millar, is a very fair man, and is doing a fine job. When the premier of Newfoundland criticized him, he criticized him wrongly indeed. I say that, and I repeat it. So far as I am concerned, not only is he a fair man but he is a just and a capable man. All I ask is that the minister and those associated with him authorize Mr. Millar to do again what he feels is right, no matter who represents the district. I do not know whether there is any authority one way or the other, but I do know that there does appear to be a great preponderance of money spent in districts represented by members who are in the Liberal party.

I should like to speak on this group of items because the information I seek is related to all of them and I think it would be wise not to ask the same question on each item. I find these figures very interesting. The total shown is $29,598,000, less unforeseen improvements of $2,000,000, which gives a total allocated to the provinces of $27,598,000. However, a large number of items are shown as revotes, either in whole or in part. For instance, Yukon and the Northwest Territories show a revote of $150,000 out of a total of $200,000. In the case of Newfoundland there is $193,000 of a revote out of a total vote of $560,000. Ottawa, out of a total vote of $5,793,000 there is a revote of $3,041,000. Quebec, out of a total of $7,968,000 there is a revote of $4,403,000. Ontario, out of a total of $4,625,000 there is a revote of $3,085,000, and so on all the way down the line. Out of a total of $27,598,000 there is a revote of $15,704,000.
Revotes of that size would indicate that these works were not proceeded with last year and I am wondering what the chances are of their being proceeded with this year. If $15 million was carried over from last year what chances are there of using $27 million this year, particularly in view of the shortage of materials and the urgent need for materials in lines other than public works? What are the possibilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Not very good, but I shall explain why we have such large revotes. These estimates are prepared in December; they come into the house in February and they are voted in June. That is when we get our authority to proceed with the expenditure. In many parts of Canada the construction season lasts only a few months. Though we have the good will to proceed we do not always succeed. If you will look over these estimates for the past forty years you will see that there have always been revotes.
What frightens me this year is the lack of materials. We may have far more revotes when I come back next time. When I prepared these estimates in December there were no restrictions on steel and with those restrictions I cannot proceed with many public works though they have come down in amount by $21 million from last year.

I have no objection to
the manner in which these figures are brought forward except that they seem to present a totally false picture as to what may be expected. Inasmuch as the taxes of this country are predicated upon expected expenditures it seems to me that here is a sizeable chunk of money which is being taken from the taxpayers when there is no expectation at all of its being used.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would not go as
far as that because a vote is transferable from one project to another. A project may be delayed or not started with, but with the authority of the treasury board we can transfer that vote to projects that are under way. Actually in many cases where there are revotes we never vote the total amount of the construction unless we know the amount of the contract. We get an initial vote, we prepare plans, we acquire a site, we ask for tenders, we give a contract, but that contract may take one, two or three years to complete. We try to have as exact an amount as possible in our estimates.
I am not a contractor, but I am told that there is hardly any way in which you can arrive at the exact amount that will be expended in one year on any project. It is an estimate. These are not costs; they are estimates. That is what my officials tell me and they are well versed in these matters. They say it is the best way to proceed, and according to the statute I must follow their advice.

I suppose it is well to
be optimistic, particularly when there are so many people to please. I understand that it is impossible to transfer funds from one department to another, but I must say that I would rather see these amounts go to the minister of resources for use in housing construction.

What is the attitude of the government in regard to a public building in St. John's? I notice there was a vote of $100,000 last year with a revote of $50,000 this year. Is it the intention of the government to have a public building erected in St. John's? There is no doubt about the need because the offices are quite crowded and are scattered all over the place.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
For the last year we
have been trying to purchase a site for this building but we have found that the people do not all agree on the site. At last I have decided that we should put the building on the government grounds, if that is the way you describe them. I have gone into the matter thoroughly but the trouble is getting
Supply-Public Works a definite price. I have to admit that I have not been successful in that. Negotiations are being carried on and the moment we receive a firm offer for this site we will have our valuators go down and make a report. When we can purchase the site we will prepare plans and specifications and proceed with the building.

Has an
offer of a site been made to the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I discussed the matter with the authorities in Newfoundland and I was shown the exact location which the provincial government would be willing to sell to the federal government. I have not received a price and I have no knowledge of the price that is being asked. I am trying to get that price.

Is the
matter being actively pursued?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As actively as I can
pursue any activity.
Where is the site?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On the hill adjacent
to the provincial buildings; I believe it is Circle road and Bannerman avenue.

I made a protest some time
ago and the minister said it was not going to be built.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Did I change my
mind? I have never visited the place myself, but I had a conversation with the highest authority in the province and he told me they would be ready to sell that site.
I take it the minister means the premier of Newfoundland offered to give him that piece of land?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I never said that he
offered to give us the land.

Did he offer to sell it to
you?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, and we are
waiting for a price.
Is that offer still open?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As far as I am concerned it is open. If they will give me a price I will get a vote and pay for it.

Then all that is stopping
the erection of a building there now is the question of price?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, no.

Then if that is not so I want to register my protest against the building being erected in the particular spot the minister talks about. If the question of

Supply-Public Works price is the only objection, that is all very well; but I still want to register my protest against the building being erected where the minister states he may erect it. The minister has to take into consideration the fact that the people of St. John's still live in St. John's, and in my part of St. John's where that building is to be erected the people do not want it erected there.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do I understand that the people of St. John's do not want to have the building erected there?
This is a residential area and it is a part of government house grounds. We still have our traditions and we still like to preserve government house grounds.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is why there is so much delay in putting up a building in St. John's.

No, it is not that by any
means. I am quite certain the minister has a lot of sites where he could build public buildings if the proper contacts are made to have the land set aside.
Whom do you have to see?

While we are considering the estimates of the Department of Public Works I should like to find out something from the minister. At page 222 of the estimates for 1950-51 there was a vote of $30,000 for the construction of a public building at Lewisporte. I should like to ask the minister why the money was not spent and why the building was not erected. I have had some communications from my constituency with respect to this matter. I have a telegram from the Lewisporte town council which I received last week. It reads:
Please advise if public building is to be constructed here this year. II not advise cause of delay.
On looking at the estimates for this year I notice that the amount has been dropped. It has not been included in the estimates for 1951-52. I should like to point out the importance of Lewisporte because it is a thriving progressive town. It is at the head of a spur of railway about nine miles long running from Notre Dame junction to Notre Dame bay, and it serves a large area. I believe Lewisporte is situated at about the most northerly point on the railway in Newfoundland. It is centrally situated in the middle of Notre Dame bay, and through it pass large quantities of merchandise including coal for the railway and a lot of gasoline for Gander. It is evident of course that it is an important place, and I am sure I do not know why this vote has not been


included in this year's estimates when the money was not spent last year. I should like to have an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can tell the hon. member right now. They took $21 million off my estimates. I had to cut some place and Lewisporte was one of the places. Hon. members will see that the Minister of Public Works is not criticized only by people from the other side of the house.
I should like to congratulate the Secretary of State on being able to get an increase of $175,000 for the building in Bonavista.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure he will acknowledge the congratulations.
The resistance was not so strong there.

The minister has explained that they needed a large amount of money for defence purposes. Of course when it comes to the defence of Canada I am all for that, and I suppose I have to suffer in my riding, but I should like to point out that this $30,000 is not a very large amount. In view of the importance of the vote and the need for it I should like to have it included in the supplementary estimates if at all possible. If not, when the estimates are being prepared for next year I hope the members of treasury board will take cognizance of what has been said, inasmuch as I understand they follow Hansard pretty closely, and see if they cannot include that vote of $30,000 so that the people in that very important thriving settlement will be able to get a decent public building. There is one other matter I should like to mention. I should like to find out the amount of money that has been spent by the Department of Public Works at Gander this year. Gander is also in my riding and is in a very important strategic position. If the international situation should become worse we can look forward to a great influx of people there again. I should like to know how mufih money has been spent at Gander. In last year's estimates there was an amount of $75,000 and in the supplementary estimates a further amount of $65,000. I should like to know the amount that was spent.

343. Quebec, $7,968,000.

I have a considerable number of questions on this item concerning the details found on page 350, "Hull-national printing bureau (revote $650,000), $1,300,000". I asked a number of questions in connection with this and received a return in sessional paper No. 107-D, dated May 17, 1951. I must say that it is notable for what I can only call its evasiveness so far as the answers are concerned. As a result I should like to ask some further questions in connection with those on the sessional paper to see if we can get a little more definite information.
4480	HOUSE OF
Supply-Public Works
The first question I asked at that time was:
What was the original estimate of the total cost of the new government printing bureau in Hull, Quebec?
The answer given is $11,300,000. The second question was:
What is the present estimate of what the total cost will be?
The answer given is $11,300,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What date was that?

It is dated May 17, 1951. Will the minister state when this original estimate was made? How long is it since there has been another estimate made, because the answer given to both those questions was the same figure, $11,300,000. In view of the fact that this printing bureau has been on the drawing boards at any rate for some considerable time, and >so far as I can see here the original estimate was $11,300,000 there should be a revised estimate now because building costs have certainly risen in the last two years.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I gave you that answer in May, 1951, I cannot see that they have gone up that much in a month.
No; what I am getting at is that the answer is quite patently wrong. The first question I asked was, when was this original estimate of the total cost of this structure made?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that $11,300,000 is the last estimate made.
When was the first estimate made?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I could give you all kinds of figures when we started off on this project. It is quite difficult to estimate before you have complete plans of the building, or to give the final figure for the work. If you asked me what the cost will be, I would say you will have to wait until all the contracts are given.

The minister has just given two different answers. He said he could not give the original estimate because you could not tell until all the contracts were in. He said the only figure he could give is the $11,300,000. Then he turns round and says he could not tell what it might be until all the contracts are in. That is the trouble with this return. Everything in it is contradictory. If the original estimate was $11,300,000, then the present estimate cannot be $11,300,000. What I want to find out is when the original estimate was made. There must have been a figure when the department first decided to build this building. They must have estimated what the total cost was going to be.
	\

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My friend wants me to say that somebody in my department made an estimate three or four years ago. Well, that is not the way we proceed. We have to start by hiring or taking on the payroll an architect, and having this architect and the departmental architects consult with the department requesting the building. Through consultation they decide what kind of building is required, and the amount of space required. They then start making sketches and plans, and as they go on they make out specifications. In a building like this one they did start some years ago-I have heard so much about the printing bureau in the house that I think it is in my own riding. Probably that is why I hear so much about it. When they started off, they did not have an estimate. I have given an estimate. Probably they did not know any more than you know or I know. My department tells me the architect says the estimated cost will be $11,300,000.

The minister is now trying to tell me, so far as I can make out, that they started the building without any idea of what it was going to cost. They start in to get architects and let contracts, and after they have gone on for a time they finally come up with an estimate. I really cannot accept that as being the way government business should be run. I do not think there is any question but that there is always an estimate in connection with any building I have ever heard about. It seems to me there must have been an estimate made so far as this building is concerned.
In any event, my original point still remains that this return is incorrect. The answer to the first question and the answer to the second question are the same. It is quite evident that they cannot be the same. Before we come to these estimates again-I see it is after eleven o'clock-I would ask the minister to get me an answer to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do not make an unfair request. When the hon. member puts a question in the house, it is sent to the officials of the department. They have the files and they have the figures. They give me the answer, and I table it in the house. If the hon. member is going to tell my officials they do not know what they are doing, I really would not like that.

I am going to repeat what I said a while ago, that this return is completely evasive. I cannot say anything more about it. There was no answer anyway to the question, and an effort was made to conceal the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw the word "conceal". It would not apply to me because I am over and above that; but I have gentlemen here who have a reputation and I must ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that remark.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot
withdraw it. The return is here for anybody to see; and I will submit it and the rest of these questions.
Withdraw.

Before this discussion is over, I will submit all the rest of these questions, and I will leave it for you, Mr. Chairman, or anyone else to say whether the return bears out the statement I have just made.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I insist that the hon. gentleman who is insulting the officials of my department withdraw that remark.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think that the hon. member for Calgary East certainly had no intention of insulting the deputy minister, the officials of the Department of Public Works or the minister himself. He, of course, knows about the citation in Beauchesne at page 105 which refers to high officials. They are covered by standing order 41 which forbids offensive language. I would think that the hon. member would himself realize that it might be advisable for him to modify his remarks or withdraw the words that he has used.
The minister and I get on very well indeed, Mr. Chairman, and I am quite sure that he knows that I had no intention of insulting him and that I had no intention of insulting his officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
